The core library lives in lib/ as single-file modules. Every module is built by make stdlib and linked into every program automatically by the lora driver.

Owned results

Functions that make memory for you return an owner: ^str, ^[]T or ^T. It is freed when your binding of it goes out of scope (or when you free it, or move it elsewhere), so there is nothing to forget; defer free(x) still works and is simply what happens anyway. An owned result lent to a call or comparison, as in strings::concat(a, b)! == "ab", is freed once that is done. release(x) gives up ownership, for code that frees it itself.

Errors

Errors are values in tagged unions, and every error says what went wrong when printed (with {}, by a failing x!, or when main returns it):

ErrorSays
nomemout of memory
io::errorcannot write: Broken pipe (EPIPE, errno 32)
fs::errorcannot open config.toml: No such file or directory (ENOENT, errno 2)
dns::errorcannot look up db.example: no such name
url::invalidcannot parse "http://a b/" as a URL: a character it cannot hold unescaped, at byte 8
textproto::unexpected550 mailbox unavailable
http::bad_messagebad HTTP message (400 Bad Request): Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding together
net::errorcannot listen on 127.0.0.1:8080: Address already in use (EADDRINUSE, errno 48), cannot read from 10.0.0.7:5432: Connection reset by peer (ECONNRESET, errno 54)
os::errorcannot change directory: No such file or directory (ENOENT, errno 2)
coro::errorcannot accept: Too many open files (EMFILE, errno 24)
strconv::invalid_number"abc" is not a number, "99999999999" is out of range for int
regex::syntaxinvalid pattern at byte 3: expected '}'
json::invalidinvalid JSON at byte 14 (/users/2): expected ',' or ']'

Each module that calls the system has its own error, <module>::error, which carries the operation (and what it was on, for fs and net) and the system's error number, errno, which tells causes apart: if (e.errno == rt::EADDRINUSE). rt::errno is that number; its constants are named like the C ones (rt::ENOENT), and rt::errno_name(n) and rt::errno_message(n) give the parts of its description. No module's function returns a bare rt::errno: it says neither which module failed nor what it was doing. Modules that only pass another's errors on keep its type: fmt returns io::error, http returns net::error. Handle errors with ? (and ? "what was being done"), !, or or; see the language guide.

Unit failures

A false requires, ensures or assert (see the language reference's Unit functions) goes to the runtime, which writes a report to stderr and stops the program, or carries on in a build made with --units=observe.

lora 
type unit_check = enum u8 { REQUIRES, ENSURES, ASSERT };
type unit_failure = struct {
	kind: unit_check,
	function: str,      // the function it belongs to, or the assert is in
	predicate: str,     // the condition, as written
	message: str,       // the message written with it, or ""
	path: str,
	line: u64,
	column: u64,
};
fn rt::on_unit_failure(handler: nullable *fn(v: *unit_failure) void) void
fn rt::unit_report(v: *unit_failure) void   // the default report

A handler replaces the report; null restores it. The program still stops once the handler returns, unless it observes failures.

mem — raw memory

lora 
@unsafe fn new(n: usize) ([]u8 | nomem)  // zeroed bytes, freed by the caller; fresh pages aren't written
	@unsafe fn release(p: *opaque) void     // frees what new or resize gave
	@unsafe fn resize(p: *opaque, n: usize) (*opaque | nomem)
	fn copy(dest: []u8, src: []const u8) void  // as many bytes as both hold; they may overlap
	fn zero(dest: []u8) void

strings — UTF-8 strings

lora 
fn from_bytes(b: []const u8) str         // a view of the bytes
	fn to_bytes(s: str) []const u8           // a view of the string's bytes
	fn at(s: str, i: usize) u8               // byte at index (not codepoint)
	fn equal(a: str, b: str) bool
	fn compare(a: str, b: str) int          // strcmp-style ordering
	fn clone(s: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)          // heap copy
	fn concat(a: str, b: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn join(parts: []str, sep: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn has_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) bool
	fn has_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) bool
	fn index_of(s: str, needle: u8) usize    // len(s) when absent
	fn contains(s: str, needle: u8) bool
	fn trim(s: str) str                     // trims ASCII whitespace
	fn split(s: str, delim: u8) (^[]str | nomem)
	fn cstr(s: str) (^[]u8 | nomem)         // NUL-terminated copy for C: pass &c[0]

strings — additional helpers

lora 
fn next(s: str, i: usize) ((rune, usize) | void)  // iterate codepoints
	fn rune_at(s: str, i: usize) (rune, usize)        // (codepoint, byte width)
	fn runecount(s: str) usize
	fn find(s: str, needle: str) usize               // len(s) when absent
	fn contains_str(s: str, needle: str) bool
	fn substring(s: str, start: usize, end: usize) str
	fn replace(s: str, old: str, new: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn repeat(s: str, n: usize) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn tolower(s: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)                // Unicode (see unicode)
	fn toupper(s: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)                // Unicode (see unicode)
	fn trim_left(s: str) str    fn trim_right(s: str) str
	fn trim_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) str
	fn trim_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) str
	fn pad_left(s: str, width: usize, fill: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn pad_right(s: str, width: usize, fill: str) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)
	fn cut(s: str, delim: u8) ((str, str) | void)
	fn splitn(s: str, delim: u8, n: usize) (^[]str | nomem)
	fn index_rune(s: str, r: rune) usize
	fn next_token(s: str, delim: u8, i: usize) ((str, usize) | void)
	fn from_utf8(b: []u8) (str | void)   // validating conversion
	fn put(buf: []u8, at: usize, s: str) usize  // copies into buf from at, as much as fits

put writes text into a buffer of the caller's, allocating nothing: what describing an error needs, as an error must be describable even with no memory left. It says where it stopped, so that the next piece follows; a buffer too small cuts the text short, and nothing is written past it.

lora 
fn describe_late(e: *const late, buf: []u8) str = {
	let n = strings::put(buf, 0, "late by ");
	n = strconv::put_u64(buf, n, e.ms);
	n = strings::put(buf, n, " ms");
	return strings::from_bytes(buf[..n]);
}

next drives codepoint iteration:

lora 
let i = 0z;
for (true) {
	match strings::next(s, i) {
		let r: (rune, usize) => { process(r.0); i = r.1; },
		void => break,
	}
}

strconv — number formatting and parsing

lora 
type invalid_number = !struct { text: str, why: str }
// "abc" is not a number; "99999999999" is out of range for int

fn utos(u: usize) (^str | nomem)
	fn itos(n: int) (^str | nomem)
	fn parse_int(s: str) (int | invalid_number)
	fn parse_size(s: str) (usize | invalid_number)
	fn parse_i64(s: str) (i64 | invalid_number);  fn parse_u64(s: str) (u64 | invalid_number)
	fn parse_f64(s: str) (f64 | invalid_number);  fn parse_f32(s: str) (f32 | invalid_number)
	fn parse_i64_base(s: str, base: uint) (i64 | invalid_number)   // base 2 to 36, or 0
	fn parse_u64_base(s: str, base: uint) (u64 | invalid_number)
	fn number_text(s: str) bool       // -1.5e+3: no +, no needless leading zero
	fn format_shortest(f: f64, single: bool, buf: *[40]u8) (str | void)
	fn shortest(f: f64, single: bool, digits: *[17]u8) (usize, int)

// into a buffer of the caller's, allocating nothing
def DIGITS_MAX: usize = 20;                       // the most u64_into and i64_into write
fn u64_into(buf: []u8, v: u64) []u8              // buf holds DIGITS_MAX: the digits
	fn i64_into(buf: []u8, v: i64) []u8          // with a '-' when negative
	fn put_u64(buf: []u8, at: usize, v: u64, width: usize = 0) usize
	// from at, zero-padded to width, as much as fits: where it ended

parse_i64_base and parse_u64_base read integers in any base from 2 to 36, with letters for the digits past 9 in either case, and an optional sign. With base 0, the prefix says the base: 0x is hexadecimal, 0o or a leading 0 octal, 0b binary, and anything else decimal. With base 0, _ may also stand between digits, as in 1_000_000 or 0x_ff.

parse_f64 gives the nearest f64 to a decimal number. format_shortest writes the fewest digits that read back as f (as an f32 when single): 1, 0.5, 1.5e+21, 1e-7; void for NaN and the infinities.

io — readers and writers

A reader gives bytes as they come and a writer takes them. Files, sockets, TLS connections, buffers in memory and every module's streams are readers or writers, so what is written for one works for each: io::copy(&out, &in) moves a file to a socket as it moves a buffer to a file. A type implements each interface by itself, and with them every interface made of them: one with impls of reader and closer is a read_closer too, and a value of a larger interface passes as any part of it.

lora 
type reader = interface {
	fn read(buf: []u8) (usize | done | failure);   // done at the end
	fn write_to(w: writer) (u64 | failure);        // has a default
}
type writer = interface {
	fn write(buf: []const u8) (usize | failure);
	fn write_vec(bufs: []const []const u8) (usize | failure);   // has a default
}
type closer = interface { fn close() (void | failure); }
type seeker = interface { fn seek(off: i64, from: whence) (u64 | failure); }
type reader_at = interface { fn read_at(buf: []u8, off: u64) (usize | done | failure); }
type writer_at = interface { fn write_at(buf: []const u8, off: u64) (usize | failure); }
type byte_reader = interface { fn read_byte() (u8 | done | failure); }
type read_writer, read_closer, write_closer, read_write_closer,
	read_seeker, read_seek_closer                 // made of the above

// every way a stream fails
type failure = (error | unexpected_end | closed | short_write | timed_out
	| too_large | invalid | nomem);
type error = !struct { op: op, errno: rt::errno }   // cannot read: ...
type invalid = !struct { at: u64, ... }             // invalid data at byte 9: why

	fn copy(dst: writer, src: reader) (u64 | failure)

// made of readers and writers

	fn at_most(r: reader, n: u64) capped             // more is too_large
	fn new_multi_reader(rs: []reader) multi_reader

// descriptors: each is a reader, writer, closer, seeker, reader_at, writer_at
type file = struct { fd: int }
let stdin: file;  let stdout: file;  let stderr: file;
fn file_read(f: *file, buf: []u8) (usize | error)    // 0 at the end
	fn file_write(f: *file, buf: []const u8) (usize | error)

	fn file_close(f: *file) (void | error)
lora 
use io;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let src = io::new_str_reader("one two three");
	let out = io::new_buffer();
	let first = io::limit(&src, 3);
	assert(io::copy(&out, &first)! == 3);
	assert(io::str_of(&out) == "one");
	let rest = io::read_all(&src, 100)!;
	assert(strings::from_bytes(rest[..]) == " two three");
}

Example: λexamples/io.lora.

bufio — buffered readers, writers and scanners

Over any io::reader or io::writer, in a buffer of the caller's, with nothing allocated. A line or token is a view into the buffer, valid until the next read; one longer than the buffer is io::too_large, never cut.

lora 
fn new_reader(src: io::reader, buf: []u8) reader      // an io::reader, io::byte_reader
	fn read_line(r: *reader) (str | done | io::failure) // without "\n" or "\r\n"
	fn read_slice(r: *reader, delim: u8) ([]const u8 | done | io::failure)
	fn append_until(r: *reader, delim: u8, out: *^[]u8, limit: u64) (usize | done | io::failure)
	fn read_byte(r: *reader) (u8 | done | io::failure)
	fn unread_byte(r: *reader) void
	fn read_rune(r: *reader) ((rune, usize) | done | io::failure)
	fn unread_rune(r: *reader) void
	fn peek(r: *reader, n: usize) ([]const u8 | io::failure)
	fn take(r: *reader, n: usize) ([]const u8 | io::failure)  // a view, not a copy
	fn discard(r: *reader, n: usize) (usize | io::failure)
	fn buffered(r: *const reader) usize
	fn reset(r: *reader, src: io::reader) void

fn new_writer(dst: io::writer, buf: []u8) writer      // an io::writer
	fn write(w: *writer, data: []const u8) (void | io::failure)
	fn write_str(w: *writer, s: str) (void | io::failure)
	fn write_byte(w: *writer, c: u8) (void | io::failure)
	fn write_rune(w: *writer, c: rune) (void | io::failure)
	fn flush(w: *writer) (void | io::failure)          // needed when done
	fn reserve(w: *writer, n: usize) ([]u8 | io::failure)  // write into the buffer
	fn available(w: *const writer) usize
	fn pending(w: *const writer) usize

// tokens, as a split function cuts them: lines, words, runes, bytes or yours
fn new_scanner(src: io::reader, buf: []u8, how: split = &lines) scanner
	fn scan(s: *scanner) (str | done | io::failure)
type split = *fn(data: []const u8, at_end: bool) (split_result | io::invalid);
lora 
use bufio;
use io;

export fn main() void = {
	let src = io::new_str_reader("alpha beta\ngamma\n");
	let buf: [64]u8 = [0...];
	let s = bufio::new_scanner(&src, buf[..], &bufio::words);
	let n = 0;
	for (true) match (bufio::scan(&s)!) {
		done => break,
		str => n += 1,
	}
	assert(n == 3);
}

fmt — printing

lora 
fn print(s: str) (void | io::error)
	fn println(s: str) (void | io::error)
	fn eprintln(s: str) (void | io::error)

	type printable = rt::any;   // any value, borrowed

fn printfn(form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::error)    // with a newline
	fn printf(form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::error)
	fn eprintfn(form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::error)   // to stderr
	fn fprintfn(w: io::writer, form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::failure)
	fn fprintf(w: io::writer, form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::failure)
	fn fprefixfn(f: *io::file, prefix: str, form: str, vals: rt::any...) (void | io::error)
	fn format(form: str, vals: rt::any...) (^str | nomem)  // owned| nomem)  // caller frees
	fn string(form: str, vals: rt::any...) ^str            // owned; out of memory aborts

fmt is a prelude: its functions can be called as fmt::println(...) without use fmt. The printing functions return io::error when the output cannot be written (a closed pipe, a full disk), so a call is followed by !, which aborts with the error, or ?: fmt::println("hi")!;. fmt::string is what a kept $"..." calls.

Each {} in form is replaced by the next value; {{ and }} are literal braces. The values are rt::any, so any value can be printed, and none is copied to do it: each argument is passed as its address and its type info. Output is gathered in a 512-byte stack buffer and written in as few writes as possible. Running out of arguments, or a malformed placeholder, aborts; extra arguments are ignored. Interpolated strings ($"...", see the language guide) expand to these arguments.

Value{}{:?}
integers, bools42, truethe same
floats1.5, 0.1, 1e20 (up to six decimals)the same
strings, runeshi, x"hi", 'x', with escapes
arrays, slices[1, 2, 3]the same
structspoint { x = 1, y = 2 }; anonymous { a = 1 }the same
tuples(1, "two")the same
enumsthe member's name, greenthe same
tagged unionsthe value held: 5, hi, not_found5, "hi", not_found
errors and empty typesthe type's name and fields: io::error { ... }, bad_input { line = 3 }the same
pointersthe address, 0x16f5a2f30, or nullthe same

Strings and runes inside arrays, slices, structs and tuples are quoted. {:#?} pretty-prints them, one element per line, indented.

A placeholder can name its argument by position, {1}, and give a spec after a colon, {:[[fill]align][+][#][0][width][.precision][type]}:

SpecMeaningExample
x X o bhexadecimal, octal or binary; negative integers in two's complement{:x} of 255 is ff
#with the prefix 0x, 0o or 0b{:#x} is 0xff
e Escientific notation{:e} of 1234.5 is 1.2345e3
.NN decimals, rounding halves to even; for a string, at most N runes{:.2} of 3.14159 is 3.14
widthat least that many runes; numbers align right, others left{:5} of 42 is 42
< ^ >align left, centre or right{:^5} of 42 is 42
fillany character before the alignment{:*^7} of "mid" is **mid**
0zeros between the sign and the digits{:05} of -42 is -0042
+a sign on positive numbers too{:+} of 7 is +7
?debug form{:?} of "hi" is "hi"
pa pointer's address{:p}

In arrays, slices, structs and tuples, the spec applies to each element: {:x} of [255u8, 16] is [ff, 10]. {:x} of a string writes its bytes in hex.

lora 
use fmt;

type not_found = !void;
type point = struct { x: int, y: int }

export fn main() void = {
	let r: (int | str | not_found) = not_found;
	fmt::printfn("{} {:?}", r, [point { x = 1, y = 2 }])!;
	fmt::printfn("{:#06x} {:>8.3} {1}", 255, 3.14159)!;
	let s = fmt::format("{:?}", ("a", 'b'))!;
	defer free(s);
	assert(s == "(\"a\", 'b')");
}

	fn now_ms() u64
	fn chdir(path: str) (void | os::error | nomem)

fn pid() int                             // this process's id
	fn parent_pid() int

	fn euid() u32                            // the user whose permissions it has
	fn gid() u32

setenv and unsetenv change and free the C library's copies of the environment, so getenv and environ return copies of their own. start_env reads the environment the program started with, which they leave alone. Its views last as long as the program, which is why config::load reads settings from it.

process — starting programs

lora 
type command = struct {
	program: str,                        // a path, or a name looked up in PATH
	args: []const str = [],              // after its name
	name: str = "",                      // its argv[0]; program's when empty
	env: []const str = [],               // "NAME=value" over what it inherits; "NAME" removes
	clean_env: bool = false,             // inherit no environment
	dir: str = "",                       // where it starts; this program's when empty
	stdin: (stdio | io::file) = stdio::inherit,
	stdout: (stdio | io::file) = stdio::inherit,
	stderr: (stdio | io::file) = stdio::inherit,
	files: []const io::file = [],        // its descriptors 3, 4 and on
	new_group: bool = false,             // a process group of its own
	group: int = 0,                      // or the group of that id
	new_session: bool = false,           // a session of its own, with no terminal
	credential: (void | credential) = void,  // the user and groups it runs as
	terminal: (void | io::file) = void,  // its controlling terminal, in a session of its own
	foreground: (void | io::file) = void,    // this program's terminal: its group in front
}
type credential = struct { uid: u32, gid: u32, groups: []const u32 = [], keep_groups: bool = false }
type stdio = enum { inherit, discard, pipe, with_output }   // with_output: stderr only

fn start(cmd: *const command) (child | start_failed | not_found | nomem)
	fn run(cmd: *const command) (status | start_failed | error | not_found | nomem)
	fn output(cmd: *const command, opts: options = options { ... })
		(result | start_failed | error | not_found | io::failure | nomem)
type options = struct { input: ([]const u8 | void) = void, limit: u64 = 0, within_ms: u64 = 0 }
type result = struct { status: status, stdout: ^[]u8, stderr: ^[]u8 }
fn look_path(name: str) (^str | not_found | nomem)

// a started program: an owner, killed and waited for if dropped running
type child = struct { ... }
fn pid(c: *const child) int
	fn stdin(c: *child) *process::pipe       // io::writer, closer
	fn stdout(c: *child) *process::pipe      // io::reader, closer
	fn stderr(c: *child) *process::pipe
fn wait(c: *child) (status | error)
	fn wait_within(c: *child, ms: u64) (status | void | error)
	fn try_wait(c: *child) (status | void | error)
	fn send(c: *child, s: signal::sig) (void | error)
	fn kill(c: *child) (void | error)
	fn terminate(c: *child, grace_ms: u64) (status | error)   // terminate, then kill
	fn release(c: *child) (void | error)     // runs on; reaped when it ends

type status = struct { code: int, signal: (signal::sig | void), core_dumped: bool,
	user_us: u64, system_us: u64, max_rss: u64 }
fn success(s: *const status) bool
	fn check(s: *const status) (void | failed)

fn close(p: *pipe) (void | io::failure)
	fn set_deadline(p: *pipe, by: u64) void  // by os::now_ms; io::timed_out past it
	fn is_open(p: *const pipe) bool

type start_failed = !struct { program: str, errno: rt::errno }
// cannot start ./build.sh: Permission denied (EACCES, errno 13)
type error = !struct { op: op, pid: int, errno: rt::errno }
// process 4121: cannot wait: Operation canceled (ECANCELED, errno 89)
type not_found = !struct { program: str }       // gcc: no such program
type failed = !struct { status: status }        // exited with code 2; ended by signal SIGKILL

// terminals
type pty = struct { controller: fs::file, terminal: fs::file }   // closed when dropped
fn open_terminal() (pty | terminal_error)
	fn foreground(t: io::file) (int | terminal_error)     // the group in front of t
	fn set_foreground(t: io::file, group: int) (void | terminal_error)
type terminal_error = !struct { op: str, group: int, errno: rt::errno }
// cannot give the terminal to group 4121: Operation not permitted (EPERM, errno 1)
lora 
use process;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let out = process::output(&process::command {
		program = "sh",
		args = ["-c", "echo hello; echo oops >&2; exit 3"],
	})!;
	assert(out.status.code == 3);
	assert(strings::from_bytes(out.stdout) == "hello\n");
	assert(strings::from_bytes(out.stderr) == "oops\n");
}

A program gets only the descriptors it is given: its three standard streams and files. Every other descriptor this program holds stays here. It starts with an empty signal mask, and with every signal at its default except the ones this program ignores, which it keeps ignoring.

look_path looks only in PATH directories written from the root. An empty or relative entry such as . is skipped, so a program is never found in the current directory by chance. To run one from there, name it as ./name. With dir set, a relative path such as ./tool refers to a file in dir, because the program starts once it is there.

output feeds input and reads standard output and error together, so a program that writes a lot while it reads never stalls on a full pipe. It also stops the program if it goes past limit (io::too_large) or within_ms (io::timed_out). io::write_all to the stdin pipe of a program that has ended fails with EPIPE; this program is not stopped by a signal.

output stops collecting once the program has ended and what it wrote has been read. If it started something in the background that keeps its streams open, output doesn't wait for that, and anything written to them later is not kept.

A child owns its process. Dropping one that is still running kills it and reaps it, so no zombie is left behind. Its pipes close with it. release lets it run on, and it is reaped when it ends. After a child has been waited for, send and kill fail with ESRCH, since its id may belong to another process by then.

Waiting suspends a coroutine on kqueue, so the other coroutines keep running. In a scope that is cancelled, the wait kills the child, reaps it, and fails with ECANCELED.

A child killed by being dropped normally ends at once. The system can hold one, though: a program whose terminal has output nobody reads can't end until it is read. The drop waits a second for it, then leaves it to be reaped whenever it does end, so a drop never hangs.

credential runs the program as another user and group. Its supplementary groups are groups, or none, unless keep_groups keeps this program's. Running as anyone but this program's own user, and setting the groups, take a superuser's privileges; otherwise the start fails with EPERM. The user and groups are set before the program starts, after its session and group, and before it moves to dir, so dir is entered as that user.

terminal gives a program a controlling terminal. It leads a session of its own, its group is the terminal's foreground, and /dev/tty is that terminal. open_terminal makes a new pseudo-terminal. The program reads and writes terminal (give it as its standard streams too), and this program reads what it writes, and types to it, through controller. Two rules come with a terminal:

  • One session each. When the program given it ends, the system takes the terminal back from everything that has it open, so each program needs a terminal of its own.
  • Its output must be read. A program can't end until what it wrote to the terminal has been read from controller.

foreground puts a program's group in front of this program's own terminal, as a shell does for a job. It leads a group of its own, unless group names one to join. Once it has ended or stopped, set_foreground(t, os::group_id()) takes the terminal back. A terminal can't go with new_group, group or foreground, and foreground can't go with new_session: these fail with EINVAL.

lora 
use io;
use process;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let t = process::open_terminal()!;
	let c = process::start(&process::command {
		program = "sh",
		args = ["-c", "test -t 0 && echo on a terminal > /dev/tty"],
		stdin = io::file { fd = t.terminal.fd },
		terminal = io::file { fd = t.terminal.fd },
	})!;
	let buf: [64]u8 = [0...];
	let n = io::file_read(&io::file { fd = t.controller.fd }, buf[..])!;
	assert(strings::from_bytes(buf[..n]) == "on a terminal\r\n");
	assert(process::success(&process::wait(&c)!));
}

signal — signals

lora 
type sig = enum u8 { hangup, interrupt, quit, illegal, trap, aborted, emulate,
	floating_point, kill, bus, segfault, bad_call, broken_pipe, alarm, terminate,
	urgent, stop, terminal_stop, resume, child, terminal_input, terminal_output,
	io, cpu_limit, file_limit, virtual_alarm, profile, window, info, user1,
	user2, stack_fault, power }
fn name(s: sig) str                      // "SIGINT"
	fn describe(s: sig) str                  // "interrupt"
	fn number(s: sig) (int | void)           // void where the system has no such signal
	fn from_number(n: int) (sig | void)
	fn supported(s: sig) bool
	fn catchable(s: sig) bool

// hears the signals it was made for until stopped or dropped
type watcher = struct { ... }
fn notify(sigs: []const sig) (watcher | error)
	fn wait(w: *watcher) (sig | error)
	fn wait_within(w: *watcher, ms: u64) (sig | void | error)
	fn poll(w: *watcher) (sig | void)
	fn stop(w: *watcher) void

fn ignore(sigs: []const sig) (void | error)    // and in the programs this one starts
	fn reset(sigs: []const sig) (void | error)
	fn ignored(s: sig) bool
	fn send(pid: int, s: sig) (void | error)     // -g: every process in group g
	fn raise(s: sig) (void | error)

type error = !struct { op: op, sig: sig, errno: rt::errno }
// cannot watch kill: Invalid argument (EINVAL, errno 22)

// ending a scope on a signal
fn cancel_on(w: *watcher) (void | caught | error)
	fn until(sigs: []const sig) (void | caught | error)   // watching from when it starts
type caught = !struct { sig: sig }               // caught SIGTERM (terminated)
lora 
use signal;

export fn main() void = {
	let w = signal::notify([signal::sig::user1])!;
	signal::raise(signal::sig::user1)!;
	assert(signal::wait(&w)! == signal::sig::user1);
}

Every watcher of a signal hears it. The signal is held until wait or poll takes it, and a watcher holds a signal only while it is running. While nothing watches a signal, it does its default, or nothing if it is ignored. That holds when the last watcher stops, too.

notify, ignore and reset refuse these with EINVAL, and a signal the system lacks with ENOTSUP:

  • the fault signals (segfault, bus, illegal, floating_point and trap), whose handlers report crashes;
  • aborted, which is Lora's own abort;
  • kill and stop, which no program can catch.

child can't be ignored, because children could no longer be waited for.

A signal that is watched is caught by a handler that does no more than write the signal's number to each watcher's pipe. It allocates nothing, takes no lock, and leaves errno as it was. In a coroutine, wait suspends on that pipe. In a scope that is cancelled, it fails with ECANCELED.

cancel_on ends a scope on a signal. Started with @go, it waits until one of its watcher's signals comes and then fails with caught. That cancels the scope's other coroutines, and caught is what the scope gives. If the others all end first, it returns and the scope ends as it would have anyway. It doesn't wait for the scope's time limit either. A scope cancelled any other way ends it too. Use one to a scope. until(sigs) is the same, with a watcher made when it starts. A signal that comes before then isn't seen, so make the watcher with notify before the scope opens if none may be missed.

lora 
use coro;
use signal;

export fn main() void = {
	let w = signal::notify([signal::sig::interrupt, signal::sig::terminate])!;
	let pw = &w;
	let r = @scope {
		@go signal::cancel_on(pw)?;
		@go {
			// serving, until cancelled
			for (!coro::is_cancelled()) coro::sleep(5);
		}
		@go signal::raise(signal::sig::terminate)!;
	};
	assert(r is signal::caught);
}
