	fn text(s: *const set, name: str) (^str | nomem)          // its value, as it would be given
	fn default_text(s: *const set, name: str) (^str | nomem)
	fn lookup(s: *const set, name: str) (info | void)
	fn visit(s: *const set, all: bool, f: *closure(i: info) void) (void | nomem)   // by name
	fn usage(s: *const set) (^str | nomem)     // "Usage of name:" and defaults
	fn defaults(s: *const set) (^str | nomem)

type info = struct { name: str, aliases: []const str, usage: str, kind: kind,
	given: bool, required: bool, env: str }
type kind = enum u8 { boolean, integer, int64, uint64, float, string, duration, list,
	count, decoded, checked, func, bool_func }
type error = !struct { problem: problem, flag: str, value: str, why: str, env: str }
// -port: invalid value "eighty": it is not a number
// -x: no such flag; -o needs a value; -db must be given; bad flag syntax: ---x
type problem = enum u8 { unknown, syntax, needs_value, invalid, missing }
type help = !void                        // -h, -help or --help, when no flag is named so
type invalid = !struct { why: str }      // a checked or func flag's reason
lora 
use flag;
use time;

export fn main() void = {
	let s = flag::new("serve");
	let port = flag::add_int(&s, "port", 8080, "the `port` to listen on")!;
	let wait = flag::add_duration(&s, "wait", 30 * time::SECOND, "how long to wait")!;
	let verbose = flag::add_count(&s, "v", "say more")!;
	let rest = flag::parse(&s, ["-port", "0x50", "-wait=1m30s", "-v", "-v", "site/"])!;
	assert(flag::get(&s, port) == 80);
	assert(flag::get(&s, wait) == 90 * time::SECOND);
	assert(flag::get(&s, verbose) == 2);
	assert(len(rest) == 1 && rest[0] == "site/");
}

Syntax.

  • A flag is written -name or --name.
  • One that takes a value is written -name=value or -name value.
  • A bool flag is written -name alone, or -name=false, but not -name false: there, false is the next argument.
  • The flags end at the first argument that isn't one, or at --. In an interspersed set, flags may come anywhere before --, and parse returns everything else.
  • - alone is an argument, not a flag.
  • A flag given twice takes the later value. A list keeps every value given, and a count counts them.

Values.

  • Integers may be decimal, 0x hexadecimal, 0o or 0 octal, or 0b binary, with _ between digits. They must fit their type.
  • Floats may begin with + or a point, or end with one. inf and nan are accepted too.
  • Durations are read by time::parse_duration.
  • A bool reads 1, t, T, true, TRUE or True as true, and the matching forms as false.
  • add_text takes text that T decodes, such as a netip::addr. parse refuses text that doesn't decode, and get decodes it.
  • add_checked takes text that its function accepts. When the function refuses a value, it says why.

add_func calls its function each time the flag is given, as parse reads it, with a pointer to the program's own state and the value: to gather -I directories, or to set several things from one flag. It holds no value itself. add_bool_func is the same for a flag that may be given alone, with "true". The function is a plain function, not a closure. A closure may reach and change anything, including the arguments parse is reading, while a function changes only what it is handed. The set keeps the state, so the compiler checks that the state outlives the set. The value it is handed is a view of the argument, so a function that keeps it copies it.

lora 
use flag;
use strings;

type includes = struct { dirs: ^[]^str }

fn include(s: *includes, dir: str) (void | flag::invalid) = {
	let copy = strings::clone(dir) or return flag::invalid { why = "out of memory" };
	append(s.dirs, copy) or return flag::invalid { why = "out of memory" };
};

export fn main() void = {
	let inc = includes { dirs = [] };
	let s = flag::new("cc");
	flag::add_func(&s, "I", "add a `dir` to search", &inc, &include)!;
	let rest = flag::parse(&s, ["-I", "lib", "-I=vendor", "main.c"])!;
	assert(len(inc.dirs) == 2 && inc.dirs[1] == "vendor" && rest[0] == "main.c");
}

Help and errors.

  • -h, -help and --help give help unless the set defines a flag of that name. The program then prints usage.
  • A flag that is not given takes its environment variable's value, from the environment the program started with, if from_env gave it one.
  • A flag that require names must be given, or parse fails with problem::missing.
  • Defining a flag twice, or with a name that is empty, begins with - or holds =, aborts: that is a mistake in the program, not in its arguments.

usage lists the flags by name:

text 
Usage of serve:
  -port port
    	the port to listen on (default 8080)
  -v	say more
  -wait duration
    	how long to wait (default 30s)

A word in backquotes in a usage string names the flag's value. Otherwise the value is named by its kind: int, uint, float, string, duration or value.

A set keeps views of what it is given: names, usage, defaults, and the arguments parse reads. The compiler checks that each outlives the set. A command with subcommands uses one set per command and parses each command's arguments with its own set.

path — paths as text

lora 
fn join(parts: str...) (^str | nomem)    // join("usr/", "/local", "bin"): "usr/local/bin"
	fn clean(path: str) (^str | nomem)       // "a//b/./c/../d/": "a/b/d"
	fn abs(path: str) (^str | nomem | os::error)   // against the current directory, cleaned
	fn rel(base: str, target: str) (^str | not_relative | nomem)   // "/a/b", "/a/c": "../c"
	fn basename(path: str) str               // "c" of "/a/b/c/"; "/" of "/"
	fn dirname(path: str) str                // "/a/b" of "/a/b/c/"
	fn ext(path: str) str                    // "gz" of "a.tar.gz"; "" of ".profile"
	fn is_abs(path: str) bool
	fn split(path: str) (str, str)           // ("a/b/", "c") of "a/b/c"
	fn split_list(list: str) (^[]str | nomem)    // a PATH's directories
	fn matches(pattern: str, name: str) (bool | bad_pattern)
	fn has_meta(pattern: str) bool
type not_relative = !struct { base: str, target: str }
type bad_pattern = !struct { pattern: str }     // bad pattern: [a-

Nothing here looks at the file system except abs, which asks for the current directory. clean is lexical:

  • one slash between names, and none at the end;
  • no . names;
  • no .. after a name it would undo, or at the root.

What it leaves empty is .. rel cleans both paths and gives a path that join(base, it) cleans back to target. That fails when one path is absolute and the other isn't, or when target is only reachable through a .. that base still holds.

In a matches pattern:

  • * matches any run of characters except /, including none;
  • ? matches one character except /;
  • [abc], [a-z] and [^a-z] match one character that is, or isn't, in the set;
  • \ escapes any character, including these;
  • every other character matches itself.

A malformed pattern is always an error, even where the name wouldn't match it anyway.

fs — files

lora 
type error = !struct { op: str, path: str, errno: rt::errno }
// cannot open x: No such file or directory (ENOENT, errno 2)

// a file opened by path: an io::reader, writer, closer, seeker, reader_at
// and writer_at, closed when it is dropped
type file = struct { ... }
fn open(path: str) (file | nomem | error)            // to read
	fn create(path: str) (file | nomem | error)          // to write, emptied
	fn open_with(path: str, opts: options = options { ... }) (file | nomem | error)
type options = struct { read: bool = true, write: bool = false, at_end: bool = false,
	create: bool = false, exclusive: bool = false, truncate: bool = false, perm: u16 = 0o644 }

fn read_file(path: str) (^[]u8 | nomem | error)
	fn write_file(path: str, data: []u8) (void | nomem | error)
	fn exists(path: str) (bool | nomem)
	fn remove(path: str) (void | nomem | error)
	fn mkdir(path: str) (void | nomem | error)
	fn symlink(target: str, path: str) (void | nomem | error)

type info = struct { kind: kind, length: u64, mode: u32, mtime_ms: i64, atime_ms: i64,
	inode: u64, dev: u32, uid: u32, gid: u32, links: u64 }
type kind = enum u8 { file, dir, symlink, other }
fn stat(path: str) (info | nomem | error)            // following links
	fn lstat(path: str) (info | nomem | error)           // the link itself
	fn file_info(f: *const file) (info | error)
fn read_dir(path: str) (^[]entry | nomem | error)    // sorted by name, no . or ..
type entry = struct { name: ^str, kind: kind }
fn open_dir(path: str) (file | nomem | error)
	fn open_in(dir: *const file, name: str, follow: bool = true) (file | nomem | error)
fn real_path(path: str) (^str | nomem | error)       // links, . and .. resolved
fn same_file(a: *const info, b: *const info) bool    // one file, by any names

// names
fn rename(from: str, to: str) (void | nomem | error)  // in one step, replacing to
	fn link(target: str, path: str) (void | nomem | error)   // a hard link
	fn read_link(path: str) (^str | nomem | error)
	fn remove_dir(path: str) (void | nomem | error)      // an empty directory
	fn mkdir(path: str, perm: u16 = 0o755) (void | nomem | error)
	fn mkdir_all(path: str, perm: u16 = 0o755) (void | nomem | error)   // and those above
	fn chown(path: str, uid: u32, gid: u32) (void | nomem | error)     // ~0: as it is
	fn lchown(path: str, uid: u32, gid: u32) (void | nomem | error)
	fn set_times(path: str, atime_ms: (i64 | void), mtime_ms: (i64 | void)) (void | nomem | error)
	fn truncate(path: str, length: u64) (void | nomem | error)
	fn write_file(path: str, data: []const u8, perm: u16 = 0o644) (void | nomem | error)
	fn write_file_atomic(path: str, data: []const u8, perm: u16 = 0o644) (void | nomem | error)

// open files
fn sync(f: *file) (void | error)
	fn set_length(f: *file, length: u64) (void | error)
	fn set_mode(f: *file, mode: u16) (void | error)
	fn lock(f: *file, exclusive: bool) (void | error)    // waits; advisory
	fn try_lock(f: *file, exclusive: bool) (bool | error)
	fn unlock(f: *file) (void | error)

// temporary files
fn temp_dir() str                                    // $TMPDIR, or /tmp
	fn create_temp(dir: str, pattern: str) (temp | nomem | error)   // "data-*.txt"
	fn make_temp_dir(dir: str, pattern: str) (^str | nomem | error)
type temp = struct { file: file, path: ^str }

// trees
fn remove_all(path: str) (void | tree_error | nomem)
	fn copy_file(from: str, to: str) (void | nomem | error)
	fn copy_tree(from: str, to: str) (void | tree_error | nomem)
	fn walk(root: str, f: *closure(e: *const walk_entry) step) (void | nomem)
	fn glob(pattern: str) (^[]^str | path::bad_pattern | nomem)
type walk_entry = struct { path: str, name: str, kind: kind, depth: usize, error: (void | error) }
type step = enum u8 { go_on, skip, stop }
type tree_error = !struct { op: str, path: ^str, errno: rt::errno }
// cannot remove build/cache/x: Permission denied (EACCES, errno 13)

info also has the file's owner and group, its link count (links), and when it was last read (atime_ms).

Writing safely.

  • write_file_atomic writes to a new file beside the target, syncs it to storage, and renames it over the target, then syncs the directory. A crash, or the program stopping, leaves either the old file or the whole new one, never part of either. Nothing is left beside it. The new file replaces what was there: a symbolic link at the path is replaced, not written through, and the file is this user's, with perm.
  • sync, and the syncs write_file_atomic makes, flush the drive's own cache too (F_FULLFSYNC on macOS), so what they wrote survives the power going.
  • create_temp and make_temp_dir replace the pattern's last * (or add to its end) with random digits, until the name is new. Files get permissions 0o600 and directories 0o700, for this user only.
  • lock and try_lock are advisory locks on the whole file, shared or exclusive. They hold until unlock, or until the file is closed.

Trees.

  • remove_all removes a file, or a directory and everything in it. It opens each directory by name inside the one above it, never follows a symbolic link, and removes links rather than what they point to, so nothing outside the tree is touched even if names change meanwhile. A path that isn't there counts as removed.
  • copy_file refuses to copy a file onto itself, by its own name or another (EINVAL), and leaves it as it was.
  • copy_tree copies a directory: each directory with its permissions, each file, and each symbolic link made again pointing where it did. It won't copy a tree into itself (EINVAL). The destination may already exist, but nothing in it may share a name with the source; nothing is replaced (EEXIST).
  • walk visits the root, then everything under it, depth first:
    • each directory comes before what it holds, and entries go by name;
    • symbolic links are visited, never followed;
    • the visit's step can skip a directory's contents, skip the rest of a directory after a file, or stop;
    • a directory that can't be read is visited again with the reason;
    • an entry's strings last only while it is visited.
  • glob matches each name of a pattern against what's actually there, and returns paths in name order. * matches names beginning with a point too. A directory that can't be read matches nothing.
  • Errors from a tree operation own the path they name: tree_error.
lora 
use fs;
use path;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let root = fs::make_temp_dir("", "example-*")!;
	let deep = path::join(root, "a/b")!;
	fs::mkdir_all(deep)!;
	let file = path::join(deep, "notes.txt")!;
	fs::write_file_atomic(file, strings::to_bytes("kept"))!;
	let pattern = path::join(root, "a/*/*.txt")!;
	let found = fs::glob(pattern)!;
	assert(len(found) == 1 && found[0] == file);
	let files = 0z;
	let pf = &files;
	fs::walk(root, &fn(e: *const fs::walk_entry) fs::step = {
		if (e.kind == fs::kind::file) *pf += 1;
		return fs::step::go_on;
	})!;
	assert(files == 1);
	fs::remove_all(root)!;
}

open_in opens a name in an open directory; with follow false it refuses a symbolic link (ELOOP) rather than following it. Opening a path one name at a time this way keeps to a directory whatever happens to the path meanwhile, as http's file server does.

time — instants, durations, the calendar and zones

lora 
// instants: moments, the same everywhere
type instant = struct { ... }            // seconds and nanoseconds since 1970, and a monotonic reading
fn now() instant
	fn unix(sec: i64, nsec: i64) instant     // nsec may be outside 0 to 999999999
	fn from_unix_ms(ms: i64) instant;  fn from_unix_us(us: i64) instant;  fn from_unix_ns(ns: i64) instant
	fn to_unix(t: instant) i64
	fn to_unix_ms(t: instant) (i64 | void);  fn to_unix_us(t: instant) (i64 | void)
	fn to_unix_ns(t: instant) (i64 | void)  // void where it doesn't fit: outside 1678 to 2262
	fn nanosecond_of(t: instant) u32
	fn wall(t: instant) instant              // without its monotonic reading
	fn add(t: instant, d: duration) instant
	fn sub(a: instant, b: instant) duration  // by the monotonic clock when both have it
	fn since(t: instant) duration;  fn until(t: instant) duration
	fn compare(a: instant, b: instant) int;  fn before, after, equal(a: instant, b: instant) bool
	fn truncate(t: instant, d: duration) instant   // to a multiple of d since 0001-01-01
	fn round(t: instant, d: duration) instant
	fn sleep(d: duration) void               // the thread; coro::sleep_for in a coroutine

// durations
type duration = i64                       // nanoseconds: about 292 years either way
def NANOSECOND, MICROSECOND, MILLISECOND, SECOND, MINUTE, HOUR: duration
def MAX_DURATION, MIN_DURATION: duration
fn hours(d: duration) f64;  fn minutes(d: duration) f64;  fn seconds(d: duration) f64
	fn milliseconds(d: duration) i64;  fn microseconds(d: duration) i64
	fn abs_duration(d: duration) duration
	fn truncate_duration(d: duration, m: duration) duration
	fn round_duration(d: duration, m: duration) duration   // halves away from zero
	fn parse_duration(s: str) (duration | invalid_duration)   // "300ms", "-1.5h", "2h45m"
	fn format_duration(d: duration, buf: *[32]u8) str     // "1h2m0.5s", "1.5ms", "0s"
type invalid_duration = !struct { text: str, why: str }
// invalid duration "5 minutes": unknown unit

// the calendar
type civil = struct { year: i64, month: month, day: u8, hour: u8, minute: u8, second: u8,
	nanosecond: u32, weekday: weekday, yearday: u16, east: i32, abbr: str, dst: bool }
type month = enum u8 { january = 1, ..., december }
type weekday = enum u8 { sunday, ..., saturday }
fn in_zone(t: instant, z: *const zone) civil
	fn date(year: i64, month: i64, day: i64, hour: i64, minute: i64, second: i64,
		nanosecond: i64, z: *const zone) instant
	fn add_date(t: instant, years: i64, months: i64, days: i64, z: *const zone) instant
	fn iso_week(c: *const civil) (i64, int)
	fn month_name(m: month) str;  fn month_short(m: month) str
	fn weekday_name(d: weekday) str;  fn weekday_short(d: weekday) str
	fn is_leap(year: i64) bool;  fn days_in(year: i64, m: month) int

// zones
type zone = struct { ... }               // owns its tables
fn utc_zone() zone
	fn fixed_zone(name: str, east: i64) (zone | nomem)
	fn load_zone(name: str) (zone | zone_error | nomem)   // "Europe/Paris"; "UTC"; "Local"
	fn local_zone() (zone | nomem)           // $TZ, or /etc/localtime; else UTC
	fn zone_from_rule(name: str, rule: str) (zone | zone_error | nomem)   // "EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0"
	fn zone_from_tzif(name: str, data: []const u8) (zone | zone_error | nomem)
	fn zone_name(z: *const zone) str
	fn zone_of(z: *const zone, t: instant) (str, i64, bool)   // abbreviation, offset east, DST
	fn zone_bounds(z: *const zone, t: instant) ((instant | void), (instant | void))
type zone_error = !struct { name: str, why: str }
// unknown time zone Mars/Base: not in the time zone database

// text
fn format(t: instant, z: *const zone, layout: str) (^str | nomem)
	fn format_into(out: *^[]u8, t: instant, z: *const zone, layout: str) (void | nomem)
	fn parse(layout: str, text: str, z: *const zone) (instant | parse_error | nomem)
type parse_error = !struct { layout: str, text: str, why: str }
// cannot read "2024-13-01" as "%Y-%m-%d": the month is out of range
def RFC3339, RFC3339_NANO, RFC1123, RFC1123Z, RFC822, RFC822Z, RFC850, ANSIC,
	UNIX_DATE, RUBY_DATE, HTTP_DATE, KITCHEN, STAMP, STAMP_MILLI, STAMP_MICRO,
	STAMP_NANO, DATE_TIME, DATE_ONLY, TIME_ONLY: str

// the compact UTC form, which some encodings use
type datetime = struct { year: int, month: int, day: int, hour: int, minute: int,
	second: int, millisecond: int }
fn to_datetime(t: instant) datetime;  fn from_datetime(d: datetime) instant
	fn utc(ms: u64) datetime;  fn unix_ms_of(t: datetime) i64
	fn iso8601(buf: []u8, t: datetime) []u8;  fn parse_rfc3339(s: str) (datetime | bad_time)
	fn now_ms() u64;  fn unix_ms() u64;  fn sleep_ms(ms: usize) (void | os::error)
lora 
use time;

export fn main() void = {
	let paris = time::load_zone("Europe/Paris")!;
	let t = time::date(2024, 3, 31, 1, 30, 0, 0, &paris);
	let later = time::add(t, time::HOUR);          // the clocks went on an hour at 2:00
	let text = time::format(later, &paris, "%F %T %Z")!;
	assert(text == "2024-03-31 03:30:00 CEST");
	let utc = time::utc_zone();
	let back = time::parse(time::RFC3339, "2024-03-31T01:30:00Z", &utc)!;
	assert(time::equal(back, later));
}

Instants are moments, the same everywhere. now also records the monotonic clock, so sub, since and the comparisons measure true elapsed time even if the wall clock is set meanwhile. wall, round, truncate and anything read from text carry no such reading. Compare instants with compare, equal, before and after, not their fields. sub saturates at the longest or shortest duration rather than overflowing.

Zones say what an instant is on the calendar and the clock somewhere. load_zone reads the system's time zone database: from $ZONEINFO if set when the program started, then the usual system directories. A name with a .. part, an empty part or a leading / is refused. Past the end of its table, a zone follows its POSIX rule.

local_zone follows $TZ as the program started:

  • a database name, or : followed by one;
  • a path to a zone file, as /etc/localtime;
  • a POSIX rule such as EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0;
  • "", meaning UTC.

Without $TZ it reads /etc/localtime, and it falls back to UTC. zone_bounds gives when the period an instant is in began and ends, both in the table and past it.

Civil times (in_zone) give the date, the time, the weekday, the day of the year, and the zone's offset and abbreviation. date goes the other way:

  • Fields outside their range carry over: month 13 is January of the next year, and day 0 is the last day of the month before.
  • A clock time that occurs twice, when clocks go back, is the first of the two.
  • A clock time that never happens, when clocks skip ahead, is taken with the offset from before the skip: 2:30 when 2:00 became 3:00 is 3:30.

add_date adds years, months and days the same way, so a month after January 31 is March 2 or 3.

Layouts have % directives:

DirectiveMeaning
%Y %y %Cyear (four digits or more, with a sign before the year 0), its last two digits, century
%m %b %B %hmonth: 01–12, Jan, January, Jan
%d %e %jday: 01–31, space-padded, day of the year 001–366
%H %I %p %Phour 00–23, 01–12, AM/PM, am/pm
%M %Sminute, second
%fa point and the second's fraction, no trailing zeros; nothing if there is none
%N %3N %6Nnanoseconds, nine digits, or the first three or six
%a %A %u %wMon, Monday, 1–7 from Monday, 0–6 from Sunday
%G %V %U %WISO 8601 year and week; week of the year from Sunday, from Monday
%z %:z %::z %#zoffset: +hhmm, +hh:mm, +hh:mm:ss, Z for UTC or +hh:mm; seconds only with %::z
%Zthe zone's abbreviation (some are offsets, as +03), or +hhmm where it has none
%sseconds since 1970
%F %T %R %D%Y-%m-%d, %H:%M:%S, %H:%M, %m/%d/%y
%n %t %%newline, tab, %

After the %, - drops a number's padding (%-d) and _ pads it with spaces.

parse reads what format writes, with a few allowances:

  • Numbers take one digit as well as two.
  • Names are matched in either case.
  • %S may be followed by a fraction even when the layout doesn't mention one.

Fields the layout leaves out are those of 0000-01-01 00:00:00. A time with an offset (%z, or %Z naming UTC, GMT, an offset such as +03, or one of the zone's abbreviations) is taken at that offset; otherwise it is a time in the given zone. An abbreviation the zone doesn't have is an error, not a guess. Every field is checked, including the day against its month, and an error says which field is wrong and why.

instant reads and writes as RFC 3339 text in UTC, to the nanosecond, in json, xml, csv and the other encodings. Reading accepts any RFC 3339 offset; lower-case t and z, or a space for the T; and a leap second, :60, which counts as the minute's last second. datetime is the older compact UTC form, to the millisecond; to_datetime and from_datetime convert between the two.

netip — addresses as values

IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (with an IPv6 zone, kept inline), an address with a port, prefixes, and hardware (MAC) addresses: small structs, copied as values, allocating nothing. The zero value of each is not valid. Parsing is strict, with one text for each value, and an error that names the byte: cannot parse "1.2.03.4" as an IP address: an IPv4 field has a leading zero, at byte 4. Text follows RFC 5952. Each type has a text and a binary form through encoding, so json, xml, csv and pack carry them.

lora 
type addr = struct { ... }        type addr_port = struct { ip: addr, port: u16 }
type prefix = struct { ip: addr, bits: u8, ... }   type mac = struct { ... }
type invalid = !struct { what: subject, at: u16, why: reason, ... }

fn parse(s: str) (addr | invalid)                    // 1.2.3.4, 2001:db8::1, fe80::1%en0
	fn from4(b: [4]u8) addr;  fn from16(b: [16]u8) addr;  fn v4(a: u8, b: u8, c: u8, d: u8) addr
	fn from_bytes(b: []const u8) (addr | void)
	fn ipv4_unspecified() addr;  fn ipv4_loopback() addr;  fn ipv4_broadcast() addr
	fn ipv6_unspecified() addr;  fn ipv6_loopback() addr  // and the link-local multicasts
	fn is_valid(a: addr) bool;  fn is4(a: addr) bool;  fn is6(a: addr) bool;  fn is4in6(a: addr) bool
	fn bit_len(a: addr) u8;  fn unmap(a: addr) addr;  fn as4(a: addr) [4]u8;  fn as16(a: addr) [16]u8
	fn zone_of(a: *const addr) str;  fn with_zone(a: addr, zone: str) (addr | invalid)
	fn is_loopback, is_private, is_multicast, is_unspecified, is_global_unicast,
	   is_link_local_unicast, is_link_local_multicast, is_interface_local_multicast (a: addr) bool
	fn next(a: addr) (addr | void);  fn prev(a: addr) (addr | void)
	fn compare(a: addr, b: addr) int;  fn equal(a: addr, b: addr) bool;  fn hash(a: addr) u64
	fn text(a: *const addr, buf: []u8) str            // buf of TEXT_MAX bytes
	fn expanded(a: *const addr, buf: []u8) str        // 2001:0db8:0000:...

fn parse_addr_port(s: str) (addr_port | invalid)      // 1.2.3.4:80, [::1]:443
	fn addr_port_of(ip: addr, port: u16) addr_port
	fn addr_port_text(p: *const addr_port, buf: []u8) str
	fn compare_addr_port, equal_addr_port, hash_addr_port

fn parse_prefix(s: str) (prefix | invalid)            // 10.0.0.0/8
	fn prefix_from(ip: addr, bits: int) (prefix | invalid)   // as it is
	fn prefix_of(ip: addr, bits: int) (prefix | invalid)     // masked
	fn masked(p: prefix) prefix;  fn contains(p: prefix, ip: addr) bool
	fn overlaps(p: prefix, o: prefix) bool;  fn is_single_ip(p: prefix) bool
	fn prefix_text(p: *const prefix, buf: []u8) str
	fn compare_prefix, equal_prefix, hash_prefix

fn parse_mac(s: str) (mac | invalid)   // 00:00:5e:00:53:01, 00-00-..., 0000.5e00.5301
	fn mac_from(b: []const u8) (mac | void);  fn mac_bytes(m: *const mac) []const u8
	fn mac_text(m: *const mac, buf: []u8) str;  fn equal_mac(a: mac, b: mac) bool
lora 
use netip;

export fn main() void = {
	let lan = netip::parse_prefix("192.168.0.0/16")!;
	let a = netip::parse("192.168.4.20")!;
	assert(netip::contains(lan, a) && netip::is_private(a));
	let buf: [netip::TEXT_MAX]u8 = [0...];
	let six = netip::parse("2001:DB8:0:0:0:0:0:1")!;
	assert(netip::text(&six, buf[..]) == "2001:db8::1");
	let ep = netip::parse_addr_port("[2001:db8::1]:443")!;
	assert(ep.port == 443 && netip::equal(ep.ip, six));
}

Maps take an address as their key with map::new_eq(&netip::hash, &netip::equal). Example: λexamples/netip.lora.

net — connections

TCP over IPv4 and IPv6, UDP, and local (Unix) sockets, as streams, listeners and datagrams. Every socket waits the way its caller runs: in a coroutine it lets the others run meanwhile, outside one it waits for itself. A deadline bounds every read, write, accept and dial after it is set (ETIMEDOUT, io::timed_out through the io interfaces); a cancelled coroutine's wait ends at once (ECANCELED). Sockets close themselves when dropped, and writing to a gone peer is EPIPE, never a signal.

lora 
type address = (netip::addr_port | unix_addr);
type conn = struct { ... }          // io::reader, writer (write_vec, send_file), closer
type listener = struct { ... }
type packet_conn = struct { ... }   // io::reader and writer of datagrams, with a peer
type error = !struct { op: op, errno: rt::errno, ... }
// cannot connect to 10.0.0.7:5432: Connection refused (ECONNREFUSED, errno 61)

fn dial(to: address, opts: dial_options = ...) (conn | error)
	fn dial_tcp(to: netip::addr_port, opts) (conn | error)
	fn dial_unix(path: str, opts) (conn | error)
	fn dial_host(host: str, port: u16, opts) (conn | error | unknown_host | nomem)
	fn dial_addrs(addrs: []const netip::addr, port: u16, opts) (conn | error | nomem)
	fn lookup(host: str) (^[]netip::addr | unknown_host | nomem) // the system's
type dial_options = struct { timeout_ms: u64 = 0, local: (netip::addr_port | void) = void,
	no_delay: bool = true, keep_alive: bool = true }

fn listen(at: address, opts: listen_options = ...) (listener | error)
	fn listen_tcp(at: netip::addr_port, opts) (listener | error)
	fn listen_unix(path: str, opts) (listener | error)       // the file goes with it
	fn listen_at(text: str, opts) (listener | error | netip::invalid | nomem) // ":8080"
	fn accept(l: *listener) (conn | error)
	fn listener_addr(l: *const listener) address
	fn set_accept_deadline(l: *listener, by: u64) void
	fn close_listener(l: *listener) (void | error)
type listen_options = struct { backlog: int = 128, reuse_address: bool = true,
	reuse_port: bool = false, v6_only: bool = false }

fn read(c: *conn, buf: []u8) (usize | error)              // 0 at the end
	fn write(c: *conn, buf: []const u8) (usize | error)
	fn write_all(c: *conn, buf: []const u8) (void | error)
	fn write_vec(c: *conn, bufs: []const []const u8) (usize | error)
	fn send_file(c: *conn, f: *const io::file, off: u64, n: u64) (u64 | error)
	fn close(c: *conn) (void | error);  fn close_read, close_write (c: *conn) (void | error)
	fn local_addr(c: *const conn) address;  fn remote_addr(c: *const conn) address
	fn after(ms: u64) u64                                   // a deadline
	fn set_deadline, set_read_deadline, set_write_deadline (c: *conn, by: u64) void
	fn set_no_delay(c: *conn, on: bool) (void | error)
	fn set_keep_alive(c: *conn, k: keep_alive) (void | error)
	fn set_linger(c: *conn, seconds: (u32 | void)) (void | error)
	fn set_read_buffer, set_write_buffer (c: *conn, n: usize) (void | error)
	fn pair() ((conn, conn) | error)                        // a socket pair
	fn send_fds(c: *conn, data: []const u8, fds: []const int) (usize | error)
	fn receive_fds(c: *conn, buf: []u8) ((usize, ^[]fs::file) | error | nomem)

fn listen_packet(at: address, opts) (packet_conn | error);  fn listen_udp(...)
	fn dial_packet(to: address) (packet_conn | error);  fn dial_udp(...)
	fn send_to(p: *packet_conn, buf: []const u8, to: address) (usize | error)
	fn send(p: *packet_conn, buf: []const u8) (usize | error)
	fn receive_from(p: *packet_conn, buf: []u8) (datagram | error)
type datagram = struct { n: usize, from: address, truncated: bool }

fn interfaces() (^[]interface | error | nomem)
	fn interface_by_name(name: str) (interface | void | error | nomem)
	fn interface_by_index(index: u32) (interface | void | error | nomem)
	fn interface_addrs(i: *const interface) (^[]netip::prefix | error | nomem)
lora 
use io;
use net;
use netip;

export fn main() void = {
	let l = net::listen_at("127.0.0.1:0")!;
	let c = net::dial(net::listener_addr(&l))!;
	let s = net::accept(&l)!;
	io::write_str(&c, "hello")!;
	net::close_write(&c)!;
	net::set_read_deadline(&s, net::after(1000));
	let got = io::read_all(&s, 100)!;
	assert(len(got) == 5);
}

A server gives each connection a coroutine of its own: @go serve(c) moves the connection c into the child, which closes it when it returns. Example: λexamples/coro_echo.lora. dial_host and lookup ask the system; dns asks the servers itself.

dns — names, addresses and records

A resolver asks the servers /etc/resolv.conf names, after /etc/hosts: over UDP, and over TCP when the answer does not fit, each server in turn, attempts times, within timeout_ms each. A short name is tried in the search domains (before or after it is tried as it is, by ndots). In a coroutine the waiting lets the others run. Names ending in .local, which hosts on the link answer for themselves, are asked of the system, as is everything when no configuration can be read (use_system).

lora 
fn system() (resolver | nomem)                  // /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/hosts
fn with_servers(servers: []const netip::addr_port) (resolver | nomem)
type resolver = struct { conf: config, hosts: hosts, use_system: bool, ... }
type config = struct { servers: ^[]netip::addr_port, search: ^[]^str, ndots: u8 = 1,
	timeout_ms: u64 = 5000, attempts: u8 = 2, rotate: bool, use_tcp: bool, edns: bool = true }

fn lookup_host(r: *resolver, name: str) (^[]netip::addr | error | nomem)   // RFC 6724 order
fn lookup_addr(r: *resolver, a: netip::addr) (^[]^str | error | nomem)     // PTR
fn lookup_cname(r: *resolver, name: str) (^str | error | nomem)
fn lookup_mx(r: *resolver, name: str) (^[]mail_server | error | nomem)      // by preference
fn lookup_srv(r: *resolver, service: str, proto: str, name: str) (^[]service | error | nomem)
fn lookup_txt(r: *resolver, name: str) (^[]^str | error | nomem)
fn lookup_ns(r: *resolver, name: str) (^[]^str | error | nomem)
fn lookup(r: *resolver, name: str, kind: u16) (message | error | nomem)   // a whole answer
fn dial(r: *resolver, host: str, port: u16, opts: net::dial_options = ...)
	(net::conn | net::error | error | nomem)
fn sort_addrs(addrs: []netip::addr) void                 // RFC 6724, in place

type error = !struct { why: failure, ... }
// cannot look up db.example: no such name
type failure = enum u8 { not_found, no_records, server_failed, refused, timed_out,
	no_servers, bad_name, unreachable }
fn is_not_found(e: *const error) bool;  fn is_temporary(e: *const error) bool

fn parse_config(text: str) (config | nomem);  fn read_config(path = "/etc/resolv.conf") (...)
fn parse_hosts(text: str) (hosts | nomem);    fn read_hosts(path = "/etc/hosts") (...)
	fn hosts_addrs(h: *const hosts, name: str, out: *^[]netip::addr) (void | nomem)
	fn hosts_names(h: *const hosts, a: netip::addr, out: *^[]^str) (void | nomem)

lookup_srv orders servers as RFC 2782 asks: by priority, then at random in proportion to weight. sort_addrs puts first what this host can reach, then those whose source address shares their scope and kind, then IPv6 before IPv4, the smaller scope, and the longer prefix in common with the source; it finds each source without sending anything.

Messages are values too. decode reads one, keeping its names (as text, with \. for a dot in a label and \DDD for other bytes) and data in a region the message owns; compressed names may only point backward, and counts a message cannot hold are refused before anything is kept. A builder writes one, section by section, to a buffer the caller owns.

lora 
fn decode(msg: []const u8) (message | invalid | nomem)
type message = struct { head: header, questions: []question, answers: []record,
	authorities: []record, additionals: []record, udp_size: u16, ... }
type record = struct { name: str, kind: u16, class: u16, ttl: u32, data: rdata }
type rdata = (netip::addr | host | mx | srv | soa | txt | unknown);
fn next_string(t: *txt) (str | void)                   // a TXT record's strings
fn new_builder(out: *^[]u8, head: header) (builder | nomem)
	fn add_question(b: *builder, name: str, kind: u16, class: u16 = INET) (void | invalid | nomem)
	fn add_answer, add_authority, add_additional (b: *builder, r: *const record) (...)
	fn add_edns(b: *builder, udp_size: u16) (void | invalid | nomem)
fn txt_of(parts: []const str) (^[]u8 | invalid | nomem)
// A, NS, CNAME, SOA, PTR, MX, TXT, AAAA, SRV, OPT, CAA, ANY; INET; NOERROR ... REFUSED
lora 
use dns;
use netip;

export fn main() void = {
	let h = dns::parse_hosts("192.0.2.7 box box.lan\n")!;
	let found: ^[]netip::addr = [];
	dns::hosts_addrs(&h, "BOX.lan", &found)!;
	assert(len(found) == 1);
	let rev = dns::reverse_name(netip::parse("192.0.2.7")!)!;
	assert(rev == "7.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa");
}

url — URLs and their parts

A URL is parsed as RFC 3986 has it, strictly: a character it cannot hold unescaped, a bad escape, port or IPv6 address is an error giving the byte. It owns one copy of its text, and its parts are views of it, as written, escapes and all; the _text functions unescape.

lora 
fn parse(s: str) (url | invalid | nomem)       // absolute, or a relative reference
fn scheme(u: *const url) str;  fn is_scheme(u, s: str) bool;  fn is_absolute(u) bool
fn user(u) (str | void);  fn password(u) (str | void)
fn host(u) str                    // "example.com:8443", "[::1]:80"
fn hostname(u) str                // "example.com", "::1"
fn host_addr(u) (netip::addr | void);  fn port(u) str;  fn port_number(u) (u16 | void)
fn path(u) str;  fn query(u) (str | void);  fn fragment(u) (str | void)
fn path_text(u) (^str | invalid | nomem)        // unescaped; also user_text, password_text, fragment_text
fn path_segments(u) (^[]^str | invalid | nomem) // each unescaped: "b%2Fc" is one segment
fn request_target(u) (^str | nomem)             // "/path?query", for HTTP
fn redacted(u) (^str | nomem)                   // the password as xxxxx
fn text(u) str

fn resolve(base: *const url, other: *const url) (url | nomem)  // RFC 3986 section 5
fn join_path(u: *const url, elems: []const str) (url | nomem)
fn remove_dots(path: str) (^str | nomem)
fn build(p: parts) (url | invalid | nomem)      // from unescaped parts
type parts = struct { scheme: str, user: (str | void), password: (str | void), host: str,
	port: (u16 | void), path: str, query: (str | void), fragment: (str | void) }

fn escape(s: str, p: part) (^str | nomem)       // part: path_segment, path, query, fragment, user, host
fn unescape(s: str) (^str | invalid | nomem);  fn unescape_query(s: str) (...) // '+' is a space

type values = struct { entries: ^[]entry }     // a query's keys and values, in order
fn parse_query(q: str) (values | invalid | nomem);  fn query_values(u) (values | invalid | nomem)
fn get(v, key) (str | void);  fn get_all(v, key, out: *^[]str) (void | nomem);  fn has(v, key) bool
fn add(v, key, value) (void | nomem);  fn set(v, key, value) (void | nomem);  fn del(v, key) void
fn encode(v: *const values) (^str | nomem)      // keys sorted: "a=1&a=2&b=x+y"
lora 
use url;

export fn main() void = {
	let u = url::parse("https://ann@example.com:8443/a%20b?q=1#top")!;
	assert(url::hostname(&u) == "example.com" && url::port(&u) == "8443");
	let p = url::path_text(&u)!;
	assert(p == "/a b");
	let r = url::resolve(&u, &url::parse("../c?x")!)!;
	assert(url::text(&r) == "https://ann@example.com:8443/c?x");
	let q = url::query_values(&u)!;
	assert(url::get(&q, "q") as str == "1");
}

textproto — lines, headers and replies of text protocols

What HTTP, SMTP and mail share: lines ending in CRLF (or LF), folded lines, headers of Key: value lines up to a blank line, bodies ended by a line of ., and replies of three-digit codes. Keys are kept canonical (Content-Type) and looked up ignoring case. A line is bounded by the buffer of the bufio::reader under the reader, a header by limits.

lora 
fn new_reader(r: *bufio::reader) reader
	fn read_line(t: *reader) (str | done | io::failure)            // a view, until the next read
	fn read_continued_line(t: *reader) (^str | done | io::failure | nomem)
	fn read_header(t: *reader, lim: limits = ...) (header | invalid | io::failure | nomem)
	fn read_dot_bytes(t: *reader, limit: usize = ...) (^[]u8 | invalid | io::failure | nomem)
	fn read_reply(t: *reader, expect: u16 = 0) ((u16, ^str) | invalid | unexpected | io::failure | nomem)
type limits = struct { fields: usize = 1000, bytes: usize = 1024 * 1024 }

type header = struct { fields: ^[]field }  type field = struct { key: ^str, value: ^str }
fn new_header() header;  fn canonical_key(key: str) (^str | nomem);  fn is_token(s: str) bool
fn get(h, key) (str | void);  fn get_all(h, key, out) (void | nomem);  fn has(h, key) bool
fn add(h, key, value) (void | nomem);  fn set(h, key, value) (void | nomem);  fn del(h, key) void
fn write_header(w: io::writer, h: *const header) (void | io::failure)   // CR, LF in a value: spaces
fn write_line(w: io::writer, s: str) (void | io::failure)
type dot_writer;  fn new_dot_writer(w: io::writer) dot_writer;  fn finish_dot(d) (void | io::failure)

type invalid = !struct { why: problem, ... }       // a header line that is not key: value: "..."
type unexpected = !struct { code: u16, ... }       // 550 mailbox unavailable

read_reply(&t, 2) reads one reply of one line or more (250-..., 250 ...): its code and its lines joined by \n; a code that does not start with 2 is unexpected, which carries the code and message.

http — HTTP/1.1 messages

Requests and responses as RFC 9110 and 9112 have them: read from a bufio::reader and written to an io::writer, with headers from textproto and bodies read as io::readers: of a known length, chunked (with trailers), or to the end of the connection.

Reading is strict where leniency lets two readers see different messages, as request smuggling uses: Content-Length with Transfer-Encoding, lengths that disagree, a coding other than chunked, a Host missing or repeated, a chunk size that is not hex or whose line or data does not end with CRLF. Each is a bad_message, which says the status a server answers with.

lora 
fn read_request(r: *bufio::reader, lim: limits = ...)
	(request | done | bad_message | io::failure | nomem)    // done: the stream ended first
fn read_response(r: *bufio::reader, method: str, lim: limits = ...)
	(response | bad_message | io::failure | nomem)          // 1xx too; HEAD has no body
type request = struct {
	method: ^str,
	target: ^str,          // as sent: "/a?b", "*", "http://h/a", "h:443"
	url: url::url,         // the target as a URL
	minor: u8,             // HTTP/1.minor
	header: textproto::header,
	host: ^str,            // Host, or the target's authority
	content_length: (u64 | void),
	close: bool,           // the connection ends after this exchange
	body: body,            // an io::reader
}
type response = struct { status: u16, reason: ^str, minor: u8, header: textproto::header,
	content_length: (u64 | void), close: bool, body: body }
type body;                 // io::reader; trailer: textproto::header, once read through
fn drain(b: *body, limit: u64) (void | io::failure)        // to read the next message
type limits = struct { header_fields: usize = 100, header_bytes: usize = 64 * 1024,
	chunk_line: usize = 4096 }
type bad_message = !struct { why: problem, status: u16 }
// bad HTTP message (400 Bad Request): Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding together

fn write_request_head(w: io::writer, method: str, target: str, h: *const textproto::header)
	(void | bad_message | io::failure)
fn write_response_head(w: io::writer, status: u16, h: *const textproto::header) (void | io::failure)
fn new_chunked_writer(w: io::writer) chunked_writer        // io::writer: each write a chunk
	fn finish_chunked(c: *chunked_writer, trailer: nullable *const textproto::header = null) (...)

fn has_token(h: *const textproto::header, key: str, token: str) bool   // "Connection", "close"
fn status_text(status: u16) str                           // "Not Found"
fn format_date(t: time::datetime, buf: []u8) str          // "Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT"
fn parse_date(s: str) (time::datetime | bad_date)         // IMF-fixdate, RFC 850, asctime
// GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE
lora 
use bufio;
use http;
use io;
use textproto;
use url;

export fn main() void = {
	let src = io::new_str_reader("POST /notes?x=1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n5\r\nhello\r\n0\r\n\r\n");
	let buf: [512]u8 = [0...];
	let br = bufio::new_reader(&src, buf);
	let req = http::read_request(&br)! as http::request;
	assert(req.method == http::POST && url::path(&req.url) == "/notes");
	let body = io::read_all(&req.body, 1 << 20)!;
	assert(len(body) == 5);
}

A server answers each connection in a coroutine of its own, one request after another (keep-alive), with what a handler writes to a responder. What the handler writes first is buffered: a response that fits is sent with its Content-Length, a larger one in chunks (or until the connection closes, for HTTP/1.0), unless the handler set a Content-Length itself; a Date is added, and no body is sent for HEAD, 1xx, 204 and 304. A body the handler leaves unread is read off (up to drain_limit) so the next request can be read; a request that asks for 100 Continue gets it when the handler first reads its body. A message that is not HTTP is answered with its status, and the connection ends. serve stops when its stop is set, from any coroutine or thread, once each connection has finished the response it is writing.

With tls set, every connection is HTTPS: the TLS handshake comes first, within header_ms, and req.secure is true. A proxy then sets X-Forwarded-Proto: https.

HTTP/2. The server speaks HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) in three ways:

  • on a connection whose TLS chose h2 by ALPN (put "h2" in the TLS config's alpn);
  • without TLS, to a client that starts with HTTP/2's preface ("prior knowledge");
  • without TLS, to an HTTP/1.1 request that asks to upgrade (Upgrade: h2c with HTTP2-Settings, and no body). It gets 101 Switching Protocols, and is answered as stream 1. Set h2c to false to refuse.

Handlers are the same: req.major is 2.

  • Streams at once: each stream's request is answered by the handler in a coroutine of its own, so a slow one holds up no other. Up to 100 may be open at once.
  • One owner of the connection: the connection's coroutine alone reads and writes the connection. The handlers ask it, over channels, to send their heads and data and to give them the body that has come.
  • Flow control: windows are kept both ways. A handler's write returns once its data has gone out as the windows allow. The connection's window is given back as data comes, and a stream's as its body is read.
  • Push: http::push(w, path) promises the client a GET of path, as if it had come with the request being answered (RFC 9113 section 8.4). The handler answers it beside the request. It is no_push if the client takes no pushed responses or this is not HTTP/2.
  • Errors:
    • What breaks the protocol ends the connection with GOAWAY and its code.
    • A stream refused, or whose body its handler did not read, gets RST_STREAM.
    • A client that gives up a stream makes the handler's later writes fail with io::closed.
lora 
fn push(w: *responder, path: str) (void | no_push | io::failure | nomem)

With gzip set, a body is gzipped when all of these hold:

  • the request's Accept-Encoding takes gzip;
  • the status is 2xx (not 206);
  • the handler has set no Content-Encoding, Content-Length or Content-Range;
  • the Content-Type is text, JSON, JavaScript, XML or SVG (compressible says);
  • the body is 256 bytes or more, when its length is known.

The response then has Content-Encoding: gzip and Vary: Accept-Encoding, and is sent in chunks. flush sends all of the body written so far.

lora 
type handler = interface { fn serve(w: *responder, req: *request) void; }
fn handler_func(f: *fn(w: *responder, req: *request) void) func   // a function as a handler
type server = struct {
	handler: handler,
	header_ms: u64 = 10000,      // a request's line and header, and the wait for it
	read_ms: u64 = 0,            // the rest of a request (0: no limit)
	write_ms: u64 = 0,           // a response (0: no limit)
	drain_limit: u64 = 256 * 1024,
	lim: limits = ...,
	gzip: bool = false,          // gzip bodies of text for clients that take it
	gzip_level: int = compress::FASTEST,
	tls: nullable *const tls::server_config = null,  // HTTPS, with this certificate
	h2c: bool = true,            // an HTTP/1.1 request may upgrade to HTTP/2
}
fn new_server(h: handler) server
fn serve(srv: *const server, l: *net::listener, stop: *thread::atomic) (void | net::error)
fn serve_once(srv: *const server, l: *net::listener) (void | net::error)  // one connection
fn stop(stop: *thread::atomic) void

type responder;                  // io::writer of the body
	fn header(w: *responder) *textproto::header
	fn set_status(w: *responder, status: u16) void   // 200 unless set; before the first write
	fn flush(w: *responder) (void | io::failure | nomem)
	fn write_text(w: *responder, status: u16, text: str) (void | io::failure | nomem)
	fn error(w: *responder, status: u16) (void | io::failure | nomem)  // "Not Found"
lora 
use http;
use net;
use netip;
use thread;
use url;

fn hello(w: *http::responder, req: *http::request) void = {
	if (url::path(&req.url) == "/") {
		http::write_text(w, 200, "hello\n")!;
	} else {
		http::error(w, 404)!;
	}
}

export fn main() void = {
	let l = net::listen_tcp(netip::addr_port_of(netip::ipv4_loopback(), 0))!;
	let h = http::handler_func(&hello);
	let srv = http::new_server(&h);
	let stop = thread::atomic { ... }
	http::stop(&stop); // here, at once: serve returns as it starts
	http::serve(&srv, &l, &stop)!;
}

A handler may run for many requests at once, from many coroutines: what it shares between them must be thread-safe. See λexamples/http_server.lora.

The client

A client makes requests over HTTP and HTTPS, keeping connections open between them, a few to each server (max_idle, for idle_ms). It takes care of the following:

  • One time limit. timeout_ms covers connecting (TLS included), sending, and the response.
  • TLS. Certificates are checked against the system's roots, or roots, as verify says.
  • Redirects, up to max_redirects. 301, 302 and 303 make a POST a GET without its body (303, any method but HEAD); 307 and 308 keep both. A redirect to another server leaves Authorization and Cookie out.
  • Stale connections. A connection from the pool that the server has closed meanwhile is found when the request fails on it, and the request goes again on a new one.
  • Sharing. Its pool is guarded, so coroutines may share one client by *const.

Over HTTPS, the client offers HTTP/2 by ALPN unless http2 is false. With h2c set, it speaks HTTP/2 to http:// URLs from the first byte (the server must speak it so). A server that chooses it gets each request on a stream of a connection the pool keeps, as HTTP/1.1 connections are kept. r.major says which was spoken. Redirects, time limits and streamed bodies work the same.

fetch, get and post read the response whole. Unless the request sets Accept-Encoding, they ask for gzip and give the body decompressed, without its Content-Encoding and Content-Length. send reads its status and header into an exchange the caller keeps while it reads the body as a stream. release then gives the connection back to the pool (dropping the exchange closes it instead).

lora 
fn new_client() client
type client = struct { timeout_ms: u64 = 30000, max_redirects: u8 = 10, user_agent: str = "lora",
	verify: tls::verify_mode = full, roots: nullable *const x509::pool = null,
	max_idle: usize = 2, idle_ms: u64 = 90000, http2: bool = true, h2c: bool = false, ... }
fn get(c: *const client, url: str) (fetched | client_error | nomem)
fn post(c: *const client, url: str, content_type: str, body: []const u8) (fetched | client_error | nomem)
fn fetch(c: *const client, req: *const outgoing, limit: u64 = 64 MiB) (fetched | client_error | nomem)
type fetched = struct { status: u16, major: u8, header: textproto::header, body: ^[]u8, url: ^str }
fn new_request(method: str, url: str) outgoing
type outgoing = struct { method: str, url: str, header: textproto::header, body: []const u8 }

fn new_exchange() exchange
fn send(c: *const client, req: *const outgoing, x: *exchange) (*response | client_error | nomem)
fn release(c: *const client, x: *exchange) void
type client_error = !struct { why: client_problem, ... }
// cannot get https://example.com/: no answer in time
lora 
use fmt;
use http;

export fn main() void = {
	let c = http::new_client();
	c.timeout_ms = 5000;
	match (http::get(&c, "https://example.com/")) {
		let r: http::fetched => fmt::printfn("{} bytes", len(r.body))!,
		let e: http::client_error => fmt::printfn("{}", e)!,
		nomem => abort("out of memory"),
	}
}

Testing handlers

record sends a request to a handler in memory, with no connection, and reads back what it wrote, as a client would. The request gets a Host of example.com, and its body's Content-Length, unless header gives them. record_raw takes the request's bytes as they are.

lora 
fn record(h: handler, method: str, target: str, body: []const u8 = [],
	header: nullable *const textproto::header = null) (recorded | bad_message | nomem)
fn record_raw(h: handler, raw: []const u8) (recorded | bad_message | nomem)
type recorded = struct { status: u16, header: textproto::header, body: ^[]u8, raw: ^[]u8 }
lora 
use http;
use strings;

fn hello(w: *http::responder, req: *http::request) void = http::write_text(w, 200, "hello")!;

export fn main() void = {
	let r = http::new_router();
	http::handle_func(&r, "GET /hello", &hello)!;
	let got = http::record(&r, http::GET, "/hello")!;
	assert(got.status == 200 && strings::from_bytes(got.body) == "hello");
}

Reverse proxy

A proxy is a handler that passes each request on to the server at base, through a client, and the response back:

  • The URL. The request's path, less strip_prefix if it starts with it, goes after base's path, with the request's query.
  • Fields. Those that belong to one connection (Connection and the fields it names, Keep-Alive, TE, Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade, and Proxy-*) are left out both ways.
  • Where it came from. The client's address is added to X-Forwarded-For, and X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto are set unless given.
  • Bodies. A request's body is read whole first, at most max_body bytes (more is 413). A response's body is passed on as it comes.
  • Redirects are passed back, not followed.
  • Failures. A server that cannot be reached is 502, and one that does not answer in the client's time is 504.
lora 
fn new_proxy(c: *const client, base: str) proxy
type proxy = struct { client: *const client, base: str, strip_prefix: str = "",
	max_body: u64 = 64 MiB }

Serving files

A file_server is a handler that serves the files under a directory by the request's path:

  • What it sends. The type comes from the name's extension, or else from the first bytes, with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. The bytes go from the file to the connection as the system can.
  • Validators and conditions. It sends Last-Modified and a strong ETag, and answers If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Match and If-Unmodified-Since with 304 or 412, as RFC 9110 orders them.
  • Ranges. A single range is 206 with Content-Range; several are multipart/byteranges; one past the end is 416. A Range that is malformed, asks for many ranges, or asks for more than the file many times over gets the whole file instead. If-Range is honoured.
  • Directories. A directory is served by its index file. Otherwise it is listed if listing is on (names escaped), and is a 404 if not. A directory's path without its last / is redirected to it.
  • What it refuses. It serves only what is under root: each part of the path is opened in the directory before it, without following symbolic links (unless follow_symlinks, and then only to where root is). So .., an escaped /, or a link swapped in meanwhile cannot lead out. Names starting with . are 404 unless dotfiles is on. Methods other than GET and HEAD are 405.
lora 
type file_server = struct { root: ^str, prefix: str = "", index: str = "index.html", listing: bool = false,
	dotfiles: bool = false, follow_symlinks: bool = false, max_age: (u32 | void) = void }
fn new_file_server(root: str) (file_server | nomem)   // a handler
fn serve_file(w: *responder, req: *request, path: str) (void | io::failure | nomem)
fn sniff(head: []const u8) str
fn html_escape(s: str) (^str | nomem)

serve_file serves one file a handler has chosen, with the same validators, conditions and ranges. It has no root, so the handler must check the path itself.

lora 
use http;

export fn main() void = {
	let r = http::new_router();
	// /static/a.css is public/a.css
	let files = http::new_file_server("public")!;
	files.prefix = "/static/";
	files.max_age = 3600u32;
	http::handle(&r, "GET /static/", &files)!;
}

Routing

A router is a handler that sends each request to the route its method and path match. A pattern is a path, after a method if it is for that method only: GET /users/{id} takes one segment as id, /static/{path...} the rest of the path, /docs/ the subtree under it, and /docs/{$} that path alone. When many match, the most specific wins: from the start, a literal segment over a wildcard over the rest, then a route for the method over one for any. A path that matches only for other methods is answered 405 with Allow; GET routes answer HEAD. A path with //, . or .. is redirected to its clean form (301, or 308 keeping the method), and /docs to /docs/ when only the subtree has routes. Two patterns of one method and shape are refused.

lora 
fn new_router() router                 // a handler
fn handle(r: *router, pattern: str, h: handler) (void | bad_pattern | nomem)
fn handle_func(r: *router, pattern: str, f: *fn(w: *responder, req: *request) void) (...)
fn path_value(req: *const request, name: str) (str | void)   // a wildcard's value, unescaped

Forms, multipart bodies and cookies

lora 
fn parse_form(req: *request, limit: u64 = 10 MiB) (void | bad_form | io::failure | nomem)
fn form_value(req: *const request, key: str) (str | void)   // the body's values first, then the query's
fn multipart_of(req: *request) (multipart | bad_form | nomem)
fn new_multipart(src: io::reader, boundary: str) (multipart | nomem)
fn next_part(m: *multipart) (part | done | bad_form | io::failure | nomem)
type part = struct { header: textproto::header, name: ^str, file_name: (^str | void), ... }
	// an io::reader of its body, which is streamed, not kept: a file may be large
fn media_type(s: str) str;  fn is_media_type(s: str, kind: str) bool
fn media_param(s: str, name: str) (^str | void | bad_media | nomem)  // boundary, charset

type cookie = struct { name: str, value: str, path: str, domain: str,
	expires: (time::datetime | void), max_age: (i64 | void), secure: bool,
	http_only: bool, same_site: same_site, partitioned: bool }
fn set_cookie(w: *responder, c: *const cookie) (void | bad_cookie | nomem)
fn set_cookie_text(c: *const cookie) (^str | bad_cookie | nomem)
fn cookie_value(req: *const request, name: str) (str | void)

A cookie is checked before it is set: a name that is no token, a value with a space, quote, comma, ; or \, SameSite=None or Partitioned without Secure are each a bad_cookie.

The request's region

http::region(req) is memory that lives as long as the request is served: whatever a handler makes while serving it goes there, and is freed all at once after the response. It sizes itself, and the server reuses one region per connection, emptied between requests, so a request costs no system call once the connection is warm. What is put in it can't outlive the request, and a handler that keeps anything of the request past it can't be made a handler.

lora 
use expanse;
use http;

type row = struct { id: i64, name: str }

fn list(w: *http::responder, req: *http::request) void = {
	let mem = http::region(req)!;
	let rows = expanse::make::[row](mem, 100)!;   // gone once it is answered
	rows[0] = row { id = 1, name = "ada" }
	http::write_text(w, 200, rows[0].name)!;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let h = http::handler_func(&list);
	let got = http::record(&h, http::GET, "/")!;
	assert(got.status == 200);
}

Binding requests to structs

bind fills a struct from a request, each field from where its tag says: @path("id"), @query("page"), @header("If-Match"), @form("email"), or @body, the request's JSON body read into the field's type (as json::unmarshal reads it, its strings kept in memory the request owns). Fields are str, int, i64, u64, bool, or ? of one; a ? field the request does not give is void, and any other is an error. A str views the request. The tags' rules are checked while compiling.

lora 
fn bind[T](req: *request) (T | bind_error | nomem)
type bind_error = !struct { from: source, why: bind_problem, ... }
// cannot bind query parameter page: not a number
lora 
use fmt;
use http;
use json;

type edit = struct {
	@path("id") id: int,
	@query("dry_run") dry_run: ?bool,
	@header("If-Match") etag: ?str,
	@body change: change,
}

type change = struct { @json("title") title: str }

fn edit_note(w: *http::responder, req: *http::request) void = {
	let e = match (http::bind::[edit](req)) {
		let e: edit => e,
		let err: http::bind_error => {
			let text = fmt::format("{}", err)!;
			http::write_text(w, 400, text)!;
			return;
		},
		nomem => abort("out of memory"),
	}
	http::write_text(w, 200, e.change.title)!;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let r = http::new_router();
	http::handle_func(&r, "PUT /notes/{id}", &edit_note)!;
}

smtp — sending mail

A client for SMTP (RFC 5321), and the messages it sends (RFC 5322, with MIME).

Connecting. dial connects to port 587 (submission) unless told, and dial_tls to a server that speaks TLS from the start (465). new_client takes a connection already made. Each reads the server's greeting.

Commands. Each sends one command and waits for its reply, within timeout_ms:

  • hello sends EHLO and learns the extensions the server offers (extension_of), or sends HELO to a server that does not know EHLO. The other commands say hello first if it has not been done.
  • start_tls starts TLS (STARTTLS), checking the certificate as verify and roots say, then says hello again. Bytes that come between its reply and the handshake are refused, as anyone on the way could have sent them.
  • authenticate uses plain, login, cram_md5 or xoauth2, if the server offers it. A password or token goes only over TLS, or to this machine; CRAM-MD5 sends neither.
  • mail, rcpt and data (or data_from, from a reader) send a message. MAIL asks for 8-bit bodies, and for SMTPUTF8 for addresses that are not ASCII, where the server takes them. Lines of the body may end in "\n" or "\r\n", and a line that starts with "." gets another.
  • reset, noop, verify and quit send RSET, NOOP, VRFY and QUIT.

A reply that refuses is rejected, with its code and text; is_temporary says whether it is a 4xx, worth trying again later. Addresses with line breaks or angle brackets are refused before they are sent.

Sending at once. send_mail connects, starts TLS where the server offers it, authenticates if given an auth, sends, and quits. send_message composes a message and sends it to all of its to, cc and bcc.

Composing. compose writes a message with these:

  • Header. Date, From, Reply-To, To, Cc, Subject, a Message-ID (made from random bytes and the sender's domain unless given) and MIME-Version. Bcc is never written.
  • Text that is not ASCII. In a subject or a name it becomes encoded words; in the body, quoted-printable.
  • Parts. Text and HTML go as alternatives. Attachments go in base64, with a name that is not ASCII given as RFC 2231 has it.
  • No added headers. A value with a line break in it is refused, so that it cannot add a header of its own.
lora 
type options = struct { local_name: str = "localhost", timeout_ms: u64 = 60000,
	verify: tls::verify_mode = full, roots: nullable *const x509::pool = null }
fn dial(host: str, port: u16 = 587, opts: options = ...) (client | error | nomem)
fn dial_tls(host: str, port: u16 = 465, opts: options = ...) (client | error | nomem)
fn new_client(s: net::conn, host: str, opts: options = ...) (client | error | nomem)
fn hello(c: *client) (void | error | nomem)
fn extension_of(c: *client, name: str) (str | void | error | nomem)   // "SIZE" -> "1000000"
fn start_tls(c: *client) (void | error | nomem)
fn is_secure(c: *const client) bool
fn authenticate(c: *client, a: auth) (void | error | nomem)
type auth = (plain | login | cram_md5 | xoauth2);
	type plain = struct { identity: str = "", user: str, password: str }
	type login = struct { user: str, password: str }
	type cram_md5 = struct { user: str, secret: str }
	type xoauth2 = struct { user: str, token: str }
fn mail(c: *client, from: str) (void | error | nomem)
fn rcpt(c: *client, to: str) (void | error | nomem)
fn data(c: *client, msg: []const u8) (void | error | nomem)
fn data_from(c: *client, src: io::reader) (void | error | nomem)
fn reset(c: *client) (void | error | nomem)
fn noop(c: *client) (void | error | nomem)
fn verify(c: *client, address: str) (^str | error | nomem)
fn quit(c: *client) (void | error | nomem)
fn close(c: *client) void

fn send_mail(host: str, port: u16, a: (auth | void), from: str, to: []const str,
	msg: []const u8, opts: options = ...) (void | error | nomem)
fn send_message(host: str, port: u16, a: (auth | void), m: *const message,
	opts: options = ...) (void | error | nomem)

type message = struct { from: str, to: []const str = [], cc: []const str = [],
	bcc: []const str = [], reply_to: str = "", subject: str = "", text: str = "",
	html: str = "", attachments: []const attachment = [], date: u64 = 0,
	message_id: str = "" }
type attachment = struct { name: str, content_type: str = "application/octet-stream",
	data: []const u8 }
fn compose(m: *const message) (^[]u8 | invalid | nomem)
fn address_of(s: str) str                 // "Ana <ana@example.com>" -> "ana@example.com"

type error = !(rejected | invalid | io::failure | net::error | net::unknown_host | tls::error);
type rejected = !struct { code: u16, ... }
	fn message_of(e: *const rejected) str
	fn is_temporary(e: *const rejected) bool
lora 
use smtp;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let m = smtp::message {
		from = "Ana <ana@example.com>",
		to = ["bo@example.com"],
		subject = "Lunch",
		text = "Noon at the café?",
		...
	}
	let msg = smtp::compose(&m)!;
	assert(strings::contains_str(strings::from_bytes(msg), "Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable"));
	// smtp::send_message("mail.example.com", 587,
	//	smtp::plain { user = "ana@example.com", password = secret, ... }, &m)!;
}

hpack — HTTP/2's header compression

HPACK (RFC 7541).

  • Decoder: reads the header blocks a peer sends, keeping the dynamic table they build up to its limit. It refuses an index past the tables, a Huffman string that is not one, a table size update that is too large or comes after a field, and a list larger than max_list.
  • Encoder: writes fields with the static table and Huffman codes. It keeps no dynamic table: its first block sets the table's size to 0, so nothing a peer's settings lower later can be broken. A sensitive field is marked never to be indexed.
lora 
type field = struct { name: ^str, value: ^str, sensitive: bool }
fn new_decoder(limit: usize = 4096, max_list: usize = 64 * 1024) decoder
fn decode(d: *decoder, block: []const u8, out: *^[]field) (void | invalid | nomem)
fn new_encoder() encoder
fn encode(e: *encoder, out: *^[]u8, name: str, value: str, sensitive: bool = false) (void | nomem)
type invalid = !struct { why: problem }  // cut_short, bad_index, too_large,
	// bad_huffman, bad_table_size, bad_integer

math — numbers, functions and the parts of a float

lora 
// constants
def E, PI, PHI, SQRT2, SQRT_E, SQRT_PI, SQRT_PHI, LN2, LOG2E, LN10, LOG10E: f64
def MAX_F64, SMALLEST_F64, MAX_F32, SMALLEST_F32: f64       // largest finite; smallest above 0
def MAX_I8, MIN_I8, ..., MAX_I64, MIN_I64, MAX_U8, ..., MAX_U64
def MAX_INT, MIN_INT, MAX_UINT             // int and uint are 32 bits

// elementary functions
fn sqrt, cbrt, exp, exp2, expm1, log, log2, log10, log1p(f: f64) f64
	fn pow(a: f64, b: f64) f64;  fn pow10(n: int) f64
	fn hypot(x: f64, y: f64) f64;  fn fma(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64) f64
	fn sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh(f: f64) f64
	fn atan2(y: f64, x: f64) f64;  fn sincos(x: f64) (f64, f64)
	fn sqrtf(f: f32) f32;  fn fabs(f: f64) f64;  fn fabsf(f: f32) f32

// rounding and parts
fn floor, ceil, trunc(f: f64) f64
	fn round(f: f64) f64              // halves away from zero
	fn round_to_even(f: f64) f64      // halves to the even one
	fn fmod(a: f64, b: f64) f64;  fn remainder(a: f64, b: f64) f64
	fn frexp(f: f64) (f64, int);  fn ldexp(frac: f64, e: int) f64
	fn modf(f: f64) (f64, f64);  fn logb(f: f64) f64;  fn ilogb(f: f64) int

// special functions
fn gamma(f: f64) f64;  fn lgamma(x: f64) (f64, int)          // log |gamma|, and its sign
	fn erf, erfc, erfinv, erfcinv(f: f64) f64
	fn j0, j1, y0, y1(f: f64) f64;  fn jn(n: int, f: f64) f64;  fn yn(n: int, f: f64) f64

// IEEE 754
fn inf(sign: int) f64;  fn nan() f64
	fn is_nan(f: f64) bool;  fn is_inf(f: f64, sign: int) bool;  fn is_finite(f: f64) bool
	fn signbit(f: f64) bool;  fn copysign(f: f64, sign: f64) f64
	fn nextafter(x: f64, y: f64) f64;  fn nextafter32(x: f32, y: f32) f32
	fn minf(x: f64, y: f64) f64;  fn maxf(x: f64, y: f64) f64   // NaN wins; -0 < +0
	fn dim(x: f64, y: f64) f64                                   // x - y, or 0
	fn f64bits(f: f64) u64;  fn f64frombits(b: u64) f64;  fn f32bits(f: f32) u32;  fn f32frombits(b: u32) f32

// any ordered type
fn min[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T;  fn max[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T
	fn clamp[T: ordered](x: T, lo: T, hi: T) T
	fn abs(n: i64) u64            // fits even for the most negative i64

The C library's libm supplies the elementary and special functions; every system Lora runs on has it, and they are correctly rounded, or within about an ulp. They are bound to it safely, so calling them needs no unsafe. The rest are written here. Special values follow IEEE 754 and C: sqrt(-1) and log(-1) are NaN, log(0) is −inf, and a NaN carries through whatever it reaches.

min and max compare with <, so where a NaN is involved, which one comes back is undefined. minf and maxf follow IEEE 754 instead: NaN if either argument is NaN (an infinity of the right sign still wins), and −0 counts as less than +0.

bits — counting, rotating and wide arithmetic

lora 
// each for 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits: leading_zeros8 ... leading_zeros64, and so on
fn leading_zeros64(x: u64) int;  fn trailing_zeros64(x: u64) int
	fn len64(x: u64) int              // bits it takes: 0 for 0
	fn ones_count64(x: u64) int
	fn rotate_left64(x: u64, k: int) u64      // right for a negative k
	fn reverse64(x: u64) u64;  fn reverse_bytes64(x: u64) u64

// what does not fit: carries, borrows, high halves (64 and 32 bits)
fn add64(x: u64, y: u64, carry: u64) (u64, u64)     // (sum, carry out)
	fn sub64(x: u64, y: u64, borrow: u64) (u64, u64)  // (difference, borrow out)
	fn mul64(x: u64, y: u64) (u64, u64)              // (high, low)
	fn div64(hi: u64, lo: u64, y: u64) (u64, u64)    // (quotient, remainder); y > hi
	fn rem64(hi: u64, lo: u64, y: u64) u64           // any hi; y > 0

div64 divides a 128-bit number by a 64-bit one. The quotient must fit in 64 bits, so y must be greater than hi; a y of 0, or one that isn't greater, aborts. rem64 gives the remainder for any hi. These are the building blocks of arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

rand — random numbers

lora 
type source = interface { fn draw() u64; }          // 64 random bits at a time
type pcg = struct { ... }                           // PCG-DXSM: small and fast
fn new_pcg(seed1: u64, seed2: u64) pcg;  fn seed_pcg(p: *pcg, seed1: u64, seed2: u64) void
type chacha8 = struct { ... }                       // the ChaCha8 stream cipher's output
fn new_chacha8(seed: [32]u8) chacha8;  fn seed_chacha8(c: *chacha8, seed: [32]u8) void
fn global() *chacha8                                // this thread's own, seeded by the system

// of any source
fn next_u64, next_u32, next_i64, next_int[S: source](s: *S) ...   // non-negative for the signed
	fn u64_n, u32_n, i64_n, int_n[S: source](s: *S, n: ...) ...    // in [0, n), without bias
	fn i64_between[S: source](s: *S, lo: i64, hi: i64) i64          // in [lo, hi]
	fn next_f64[S: source](s: *S) f64;  fn next_f32[S: source](s: *S) f32   // in [0, 1)
	fn norm_f64[S: source](s: *S) f64     // normal: mean 0, deviation 1
	fn exp_f64[S: source](s: *S) f64      // exponential: rate 1
	fn perm[S: source](s: *S, n: int) (^[]int | nomem)
	fn shuffle[S: source](s: *S, n: int, swap: *closure(i: int, j: int) void) void
	fn shuffle_slice[S: source, T](s: *S, xs: []T) void
	fn fill[S: source](s: *S, buf: []u8) void
type zipf = struct { ... }
fn new_zipf(q: f64, v: f64, max: u64) (zipf | void)   // q > 1, v >= 1
	fn next_zipf[S: source](z: *const zipf, s: *S) u64
lora 
use rand;

export fn main() void = {
	let r = rand::new_pcg(1, 2);              // the same numbers every run
	let die = rand::int_n(&r, 6) + 1;
	assert(die >= 1 && die <= 6);
	let coin = rand::next_f64(rand::global()) < 0.5;
	let order = rand::perm(&r, 10)!;
	assert(len(order) == 10);
}

Use these for simulations, sampling, tests and games. Anything an attacker must not guess, such as keys or tokens, needs crypto::random.

A source seeded the same way gives the same numbers on every system:

  • pcg is a 128-bit permuted congruential generator with the DXSM output function;
  • chacha8 is the ChaCha stream cipher with 8 rounds, its key the seed.

global() is the calling thread's own chacha8, seeded from the system the first time it's used. Ranges are drawn without modulo bias, and floats are spread evenly over every representable value they can take.

big — integers, rationals and floats of any size

	fn parse(s: str, base: uint) (integer | invalid | nomem)   // base 2 to MAX_BASE (62), or 0: by prefix
