type invalid = !struct { text: str, base: uint }
// "12x4" is not a number in base 10
lora 
use big;

export fn main() void = {
	let a = big::parse("123456789012345678901234567890", 10)!;
	let b = big::from_i64(-42)!;
	let p = big::mul(&a, &b)!;
	let t = big::text(&p, 10)!;
	assert(t == "-5185185138518518513851851851380");
	let third = big::from_frac(1, 3)!;
	let x = big::float_from_ratio(&third, 200, big::rounding::nearest_even)!;
	let digits = big::float_text(&x, 'g', 30)!;
	assert(digits == "0.333333333333333333333333333333");
}

Every value owns its digits, and every operation returns a new value, so nothing a caller holds ever changes under it.

Integers.

  • Multiplication switches to Karatsuba's method once both numbers pass 24 limbs. Division is Knuth's algorithm D for divisors under 60 limbs, and Burnikel and Ziegler's recursive division above that, which works through multiplications and so gains from Karatsuba's method.
  • Text and parsing split a large number in halves by powers of the base, so they also cost a few multiplications and divisions rather than one pass per digit chunk: hundreds of thousands of digits take under a second.
  • Bitwise operations treat negatives as infinite two's complement, so -1 is all ones.
  • probably_prime combines Miller–Rabin to base 2, n more random bases, and an extra strong Lucas test. Together that's Baillie–PSW, which no composite number is known to pass.
  • Text uses bases 2 to 62, with digits past 9 written a–z then A–Z. With base 0, the prefix chooses the base, and _ may separate digits.
  • divide rounds the quotient toward zero, down, to the nearest or up, and returns the remainder that goes with it.

Rationals stay in lowest terms, with a positive denominator. Every finite f64 is a rational exactly, and ratio_to_f64 rounds once to the nearest, subnormals and infinity included.

Floats keep their precision in bits, a rounding mode, and the accuracy of the operation that produced them: exact, or rounded below or above. An operation's result takes the larger of its operands' precisions and the first operand's rounding mode. It is computed exactly to enough bits, then rounded once. with_prec rounds to another precision or mode.

Infinities follow IEEE 754. There is no NaN, so inf − inf, 0 × inf, 0 / 0, inf / inf and the square root of a negative number abort. Past exponent 2³¹ a result is ±inf, and below −2³¹ it is ±0.

parse_float reads decimals; parse_float_base also takes mantissas in base 2, 8 or 16, by a 0b, 0o or 0x prefix with base 0, and an exponent of p for a power of 2: 0x1.8p3 is 12. With base 0, _ may separate digits. An exponent too large to compute exactly gives ±inf or ±0 at once, or rounds through a power of ten made 128 bits beyond the precision. float_to_i64 and float_to_u64 cut toward zero and clamp to the type's range, with the accuracy saying which way the result lies from x.

float_text makes only the decimal digits it writes, each correct: one division gives the leading digits, with a note of whether anything follows them, so a float's exponent costs little however large it is. With digits of −1 it writes the fewest digits that read back as the same float at its precision, found between the halfway points to the float's neighbours; for 53 bits that is the same as a shortest f64. Fixed digits are rounded half to even.

cmplx — complex numbers

lora 
type complex = struct { re: f64, im: f64 }
fn new(re: f64, im: f64) complex;  fn inf() complex;  fn nan() complex
	fn is_inf(z: complex) bool;  fn is_nan(z: complex) bool;  fn equal(a, b: complex) bool
	fn add, sub, mul, div(a: complex, b: complex) complex;  fn neg, conj(a: complex) complex
	fn scale(a: complex, k: f64) complex
	fn abs(z) f64;  fn phase(z) f64;  fn polar(z) (f64, f64);  fn rect(r: f64, theta: f64) complex
	fn sqrt, exp, log, log10(z: complex) complex;  fn pow(x: complex, y: complex) complex
	fn sin, cos, tan, cot, sinh, cosh, tanh(z: complex) complex
	fn asin, acos, atan, asinh, acosh, atanh(z: complex) complex
	fn text(z: complex) (^str | nomem)            // "(1+2i)"
type complex32 = struct { re: f32, im: f32 }
fn new32(re: f32, im: f32) complex32;  fn widen(z: complex32) complex;  fn narrow(z: complex) complex32
	fn parse(s: str) (complex | invalid)           // "(1+2i)", "3i", "1e3-4i"

Infinities, NaN and signed zeros follow C's Annex G:

  • A complex number with an infinite part counts as infinite, even if the other part is NaN.
  • Square roots, logarithms and the inverse functions take the sign of a zero imaginary part into account at their branch cuts.
  • div uses Smith's method, so a quotient that fits never overflows partway through.
  • Near its poles, tan and cot use a series with π split in three parts, so they stay accurate there.

complex32 stores a complex number in half the room. Widen it to compute, and narrow the result, which rounds each part to the nearest f32.

compare — orders of numbers, strings and slices

An order says which of two values comes first: less, equal or greater.

  • Numbers and runes: any type ordered with < compares with of. Floats are in a total order: NaN comes before every other value and equals itself, so sorting gathers NaNs at the start instead of scattering them. -0.0 and 0.0 are equal.
  • Sorting: less and greater are that order as functions for sort::sort_by (&compare::less::[f64], or greater for largest first). min, max, clamp, min_of and max_of use the same order.
  • Strings:
    • text compares bytes (code points, for UTF-8);
    • fold treats ASCII letters in either case alike;
    • natural compares each run of digits by the number it is, so "file2" comes before "file10" and "v1.9" before "v1.10". The digit runs can be of any length. Of two names that differ only in leading zeros, the one with fewer comes first.
  • Slices: slices compares element by element, in of's order, and a prefix comes first. slices_by does the same with a comparison of your own, and same tells whether two slices hold the same elements.
  • Chaining: then sorts by one thing, then another; reverse turns an order around.

Runes compare too, by code point, as < orders them.

lora 
type order = enum i8 { less = -1, equal = 0, greater = 1 }
fn of[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) order
fn less[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) bool          // for sort::sort_by
fn greater[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) bool
fn min[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T;    fn max[T: ordered](a: T, b: T) T
fn clamp[T: ordered](x: T, lo: T, hi: T) T  // requires lo <= hi
fn min_of[T: ordered](xs: []const T) (T | void);    fn max_of[T: ordered](xs: []const T) (T | void)
fn then(first: order, next: order) order
fn reverse(o: order) order
fn sign(o: order) int                        // -1, 0, 1
fn slices[T: ordered](a: []const T, b: []const T) order
fn slices_by[T](a: []const T, b: []const T, cmp: *fn(x: *const T, y: *const T) order) order
fn same[T: equatable](a: []const T, b: []const T) bool
fn text(a: str, b: str) order               // by bytes
fn fold(a: str, b: str) order               // ASCII letters in either case alike
fn natural(a: str, b: str) order            // "file2" before "file10"
lora 
use compare;
use sort;

type person = struct { last: str, first: str }

fn by_name(a: person, b: person) bool =
	compare::then(compare::text(a.last, b.last), compare::text(a.first, b.first))
		== compare::order::less;

export fn main() void = {
	let people = [person { last = "Lee", first = "Bo" }, person { last = "Ada", first = "Zed" },
		person { last = "Lee", first = "Al" }];
	sort::sort_by(people, &by_name);
	assert(people[0].last == "Ada" && people[1].first == "Al");

	let files = ["file10", "file2", "file1"];
	sort::sort_by(files, &natural_less);
	assert(files[0] == "file1" && files[2] == "file10");
	assert(compare::clamp(15, 0, 10) == 10);
}

fn natural_less(a: str, b: str) bool = compare::natural(a, b) == compare::order::less;

sort — generic sorting and searching

lora 
fn sort[T](vals: []T) void                                  // ascending by <
	fn reverse_sort[T](vals: []T) void                          // descending
	fn sort_by[T](vals: []T, less: *fn(a: T, b: T) bool) void
	fn sort_unstable[T](vals: []T) void
	fn sort_unstable_by[T](vals: []T, less: *fn(a: T, b: T) bool) void
	fn is_sorted[T](vals: []T) bool
	fn search[T](vals: []T, x: T) (usize | void)                 // binary search
	fn lower_bound[T](vals: []T, x: T) usize                     // insertion point
	fn sort_str(vals: []str) void                               // byte-wise order
	fn str_less(a: str, b: str) bool
	fn sort_size(vals: []usize) void                             // = sort, kept for old callers
	fn sort_f64(vals: []f64) void

sort, reverse_sort and sort_by are stable: equal elements keep their order, so sorting by one key and then by another keeps the first order within the second. They are merge sorts, O(n log n), using memory as big as the slice while they run. If there is none they merge in place, in O(n log² n), so they never fail. sort of whole numbers uses the unstable sort, as equal numbers can't be told apart.

sort_unstable and sort_unstable_by allocate nothing, and don't promise the order of equal elements. They are introsorts: median-of-three quicksort, insertion sort for runs of 16 or fewer, and heapsort when recursion exceeds 2·log2(n), and O(n log n) in the worst case.

lora 
def FNV_OFFSET: u64
	def FNV_PRIME: u64
	fn fnv1a(data: []u8) u64
	fn fnv1a_str(s: str) u64
	fn combine(h: u64, data: []u8) u64   // fold more data into a hash

fn crc32(data: []const u8) u32                   // as gzip, zip and PNG check
fn crc32_update(crc: u32, data: []const u8) u32  // going on from crc (0 at first)
fn adler32(data: []const u8) u32                 // as zlib checks
fn adler32_update(a: u32, data: []const u8) u32  // going on from a (1 at first)

compress — DEFLATE, gzip and zlib

Streams of DEFLATE (RFC 1951), and of the gzip (RFC 1952) and zlib (RFC 1950) formats around it.

Reading. An inflater, gzip_reader or zlib_reader is an io::reader that decompresses what it reads from its source:

  • A gzip stream may hold many members, one after another, and each is checked by its CRC-32 and length. A zlib stream is checked by its Adler-32.
  • Data that is not a stream, or does not check, is io::invalid, at the byte it was found. A stream cut short is io::unexpected_end.
  • A read gives what has come out once a block ends, so a stream flushed partway can be read up to the flush.

Writing. A deflater, gzip_writer or zlib_writer is an io::writer that compresses what is written to it, at a level from STORE (0) to SMALLEST (9):

  • Each block is coded in whichever is smallest: dynamic codes, fixed codes, or stored.
  • flush, flush_gzip or the zlib writer's flush(&w.d) sends what was written so far, so a reader can have all of it. The stream goes on after.
  • finish, finish_gzip or finish_zlib ends the stream.
  • With void for the destination, what is made is kept: output gives it, and clear_output clears it once it has been sent on.
lora 
def STORE: int = 0;  def FASTEST: int = 1;  def DEFAULT: int = 6;  def SMALLEST: int = 9;

fn new_inflater(src: io::reader) inflater
fn new_gzip_reader(src: io::reader) gzip_reader
	fn gzip_name(g: *const gzip_reader) str     // the name the header gives, or ""
fn new_zlib_reader(src: io::reader) zlib_reader

fn new_deflater(dst: (io::writer | void), level: int = DEFAULT) (deflater | nomem)
	fn flush(d: *deflater) (void | io::failure)
	fn finish(d: *deflater) (void | io::failure)
	fn output(d: *const deflater) []const u8    // with no dst: what is made
	fn clear_output(d: *deflater) void
fn new_gzip_writer(dst: (io::writer | void), level: int = DEFAULT, name: str = "")
	(gzip_writer | io::failure | nomem)          // its deflater is g.d
	fn flush_gzip(g: *gzip_writer) (void | io::failure)
	fn finish_gzip(g: *gzip_writer) (void | io::failure)
fn new_zlib_writer(dst: (io::writer | void), level: int = DEFAULT) (zlib_writer | io::failure | nomem)
	fn finish_zlib(w: *zlib_writer) (void | io::failure)
lora 
use compress;
use io;
use strings;

export fn main() void = {
	let packed = io::new_buffer();
	let g = compress::new_gzip_writer(&packed)!;
	io::write_all(&g, strings::to_bytes("hello, hello, hello"))!;
	compress::finish_gzip(&g)!;

	let src = io::new_bytes_reader(io::bytes_of(&packed));
	let r = compress::new_gzip_reader(&src);
	let back = io::read_all(&r, 1 << 20)!;
	assert(strings::from_bytes(back) == "hello, hello, hello");
}

tar — tape archives

Files one after another, each a 512-byte header and its data.

lora 
type header = struct { name: str, linkname: str, kind: kind, typeflag: u8, length: i64,
	mode: u32, uid: i64, gid: i64, uname: str, gname: str, mtime: (time::instant | void),
	atime: (time::instant | void), ctime: (time::instant | void), devmajor: i64, devminor: i64,
	pax: str, format: format }
type kind = enum u8 { file, hard_link, symlink, char_device, block_device, dir, fifo, global, other }
fn new_reader(src: io::reader) reader                // an io::reader of each entry's data
	fn next(r: *reader) (header | done | io::failure | nomem)
fn new_writer(dst: io::writer) writer                // an io::writer of each entry's data
	fn write_header(w: *writer, h: *const header) (void | io::failure | nomem)
	fn close(w: *writer) (void | io::failure)
fn pax_records(text: str) ((str, str, str) | done | io::invalid)   // key, value, the rest
	fn pax_add(out: *^[]u8, key: str, value: str) (void | nomem)
lora 
use io;
use strings;
use tar;

export fn main() void = {
	let out = io::new_buffer();
	let w = tar::new_writer(&out);
	tar::write_header(&w, &tar::header { name = "hello.txt", length = 5, ... })!;
	io::write_all(&w, strings::to_bytes("hello"))!;
	tar::close(&w)!;
	let src = io::new_bytes_reader(io::bytes_of(&out));
	let r = tar::new_reader(&src);
	let h = tar::next(&r)! as tar::header;
	assert(h.name == "hello.txt" && h.length == 5);
	assert(tar::next(&r)! is done);
}

next reads the V7, USTAR, PAX and GNU formats:

  • PAX records override what the header holds: path, size, ids, names, and times with their fractions. Global records apply to every entry after them, and are given as an entry of kind::global themselves.
  • GNU's long names and links, and its base-256 numbers, are read.
  • So are sparse files, in old GNU's form and in PAX's 0.0, 0.1 and 1.0; their holes read as zeros.
  • A header's strings are views into the reader, good until the next next. The data an entry leaves unread is skipped.
  • A checksum that does not match is io::invalid, at the byte where the header is. A PAX header or long name of more than 1 MiB is refused, so an archive cannot make the reader take memory without end.

write_header writes USTAR, splitting a long name between its name and prefix fields where it can. It adds PAX records for what USTAR cannot hold: long or non-ASCII names, large numbers, fractional times, and access and change times. Writing more data than the header's length is io::too_large, and less is refused at the next header.

zip — ZIP archives

Files stored or deflated, each named in a central directory at the end.

lora 
fn open(src: io::reader_at, length: u64) (archive | io::failure | nomem)
	fn count(a: *const archive) usize;  fn file_at(a: *const archive, i: usize) file
	fn comment(a: *const archive) str
	fn raw(a: *const archive, f: *const file) (section | io::failure)   // the data as stored
	fn entry(raw: *section, f: *const file) (entry_reader | io::invalid)  // as it was
	fn data_offset(s: *const section) u64;  fn is_dir(f: *const file) bool
type file = struct { name: str, comment: str, method: u16, flags: u16, crc32: u32,
	compressed: u64, uncompressed: u64, modified: time::instant, mode: u32,
	extra: []u8, header_at: u64, creator: u8 }
fn new_writer(dst: io::writer) writer                // an io::writer of each file's data
	fn create(w: *writer, h: *const file_header) (void | io::failure | nomem)
	fn set_comment(w: *writer, c: str) (void | io::invalid | nomem)
	fn close(w: *writer) (void | io::failure | nomem)
type file_header = struct { name: str, comment: str = "", method: method = method::deflate,
	level: int = compress::DEFAULT, modified: (time::instant | void) = void, mode: u32 = 0 }
type method = enum u16 { store = 0, deflate = 8 }
lora 
use io;
use strings;
use zip;

export fn main() void = {
	let out = io::new_buffer();
	let w = zip::new_writer(&out);
	zip::create(&w, &zip::file_header { name = "hello.txt", ... })!;
	io::write_all(&w, strings::to_bytes("hello, hello, hello"))!;
	zip::close(&w)!;
	let src = io::new_bytes_reader(io::bytes_of(&out));
	let a = zip::open(&src, @u64(len(io::bytes_of(&out))))!;
	let f = zip::file_at(&a, 0);
	let raw = zip::raw(&a, &f)!;
	let r = zip::entry(&raw, &f)!;
	let buf: [64]u8 = [0...];
	let n = r.read(buf[..])! as usize;
	assert(strings::from_bytes(buf[..n]) == "hello, hello, hello");
}

Reading:

  • open finds the end record, and ZIP64's where there is one, which covers files past 4 GiB and more than 65535 of them.
  • Times come from MS-DOS's fields (taken as UTC), or more exactly from the extended timestamp or NTFS's field where a file has one.
  • A file's mode is read from Unix's attributes, or made from MS-DOS's.
  • raw checks the local header, and entry reads the data, stored or deflated. At the end it checks the length and CRC-32 against the central directory's; a mismatch is io::invalid. Encrypted files, and methods other than store and deflate, are refused.
  • A file's strings are views into the archive.

Writing:

  • create begins a file, and what is written to the writer then is its data, until the next create or close.
  • Sizes and CRC-32 go in a descriptor after the data, so nothing needs to seek back.
  • Names and comments that are not ASCII are flagged as UTF-8. The time goes in an extended timestamp as well as MS-DOS's fields.
  • close writes the central directory, with ZIP64's records where sizes, offsets or the number of files need them.

utf8 — UTF-8 validation, decoding, encoding

lora 
fn valid(c: rune) bool
	fn validate(s: str) bool              // rejects overlong/surrogate/out-of-range
	fn count(s: str) usize                 // codepoints, not bytes
	fn decode(s: str) (^[]rune | nomem)
	fn encode(rs: []rune) (^[]u8 | nomem)
	fn encode_rune(b: []u8, pos: usize, c: rune) usize

map — generic hash maps

lora 
type map[K, V] = struct { … }
fn new[K, V](hashfn: *fn(k: K) u64) map[K, V]                 // keys compared by ==
	fn new_eq[K, V](hashfn: *fn(k: K) u64, eqfn: *fn(a: K, b: K) bool) map[K, V]
	fn finish[K, V](m: *map[K, V]) void
	fn put[K, V](m: *map[K, V], k: K, v: V) (void | nomem)   // insert or replace
	fn get[K, V](m: *map[K, V], k: K) nullable *V            // null if absent
	fn contains[K, V](m: *map[K, V], k: K) bool
	fn remove[K, V](m: *map[K, V], k: K) bool                // true if it was present
	fn count[K, V](m: *map[K, V]) usize
	fn clear[K, V](m: *map[K, V]) void                       // keeps the memory
	fn iter[K, V](m: *map[K, V]) iterator[K, V]
	fn next[K, V](it: *iterator[K, V]) ((K, *V) | done)
	fn read[K, V](m: *const map[K, V]) reading[K, V]           // only reads it
	fn next_read[K, V](it: *reading[K, V]) ((K, *const V) | done)

	fn hash_str(s: str) u64      // also hash_int, hash_uint, hash_i64, hash_u64,
	fn mix(x: u64) u64           // hash_i32, hash_u32, hash_size, hash_rune

A map owns its table, freed when the map is dropped, not what is in it: its keys and values can't own memory (a map of ^str is refused, rather than leaking them). A key or value that views something, such as a str, is a view the map holds: the map can't be used once what it views has ended.

lora 
let ages: map::map[str, int] = map::new(&map::hash_str);
map::put(&ages, "ada", 36)!;
match map::get(&ages, "ada") {
	null => abort(),
	let age: *int => *age += 1,
}

let it = map::iter(&ages);
for (true) {
	match map::next(&it) {
		done => break,
		let kv: (str, *int) => fmt::println(kv.0)!,
	}
}

With new, keys can be any type that supports ==: integers, runes, bools, strings, pointers. For other keys, such as structs, use new_eq with an equality function. Lora has no traits, so the hash function is passed in. Write your own for other key types, ideally ending in map::mix. The map uses open addressing with linear probing, stays at most 3/4 full, and grows by doubling. Removal shifts entries back instead of leaving tombstones. Nothing is allocated until the first put. Keys and values are stored by value and never freed by the map. Pointers from get and iteration are invalidated by the next put or remove, and the map must not change while it is iterated. Roughly 110 ns per operation for 1M int keys on an M-series Mac, including growth.

set — generic hash sets

lora 
type set[T] = struct { … }                      // a map::map[T, bool]
fn new[T](hashfn: *fn(k: T) u64) set[T]
	fn new_eq[T](hashfn: *fn(k: T) u64, eqfn: *fn(a: T, b: T) bool) set[T]
	fn finish[T](s: *set[T]) void
	fn add[T](s: *set[T], x: T) (bool | nomem)      // true if newly added
	fn contains[T](s: *set[T], x: T) bool
	fn remove[T](s: *set[T], x: T) bool
	fn count[T](s: *set[T]) usize
	fn clear[T](s: *set[T]) void
	fn iter[T](s: *set[T]) iterator[T]
	fn next[T](it: *iterator[T]) (T | done)

Sets take the same hash functions: set::new(&map::hash_str).

pool — values reached by handles

A pool keeps values of one type in slots, and gives a handle for each: the slot's number and its generation, not a pointer. Removing a value moves its slot's generation on, so every handle to it stops working: a stale handle finds nothing, never what took its place. Things that point at each other (a graph, a tree with parent links, a scene's entities) keep handles, with no unsafe code and no owners in a cycle.

lora 
type pool[T] = struct { … }
type handle[T] = struct { index: u32, gen: u32, pool: u32 }
fn new[T]() pool[T]                                  // allocates nothing yet
fn put[T](p: *pool[T], v: T) (handle[T] | nomem)
fn get[T](p: *pool[T], h: handle[T]) nullable *T     // null once removed
fn contains[T](p: *pool[T], h: handle[T]) bool
fn take[T](p: *pool[T], h: handle[T]) (T | void)     // moves the value out
fn remove[T](p: *pool[T], h: handle[T]) bool         // drops the value
fn count[T](p: *pool[T]) usize
fn clear[T](p: *pool[T]) void                        // drops all; every handle ends
fn finish[T](p: *pool[T]) void                       // and frees the slots
fn iter[T](p: *pool[T]) iterator[T]
fn next[T](it: *iterator[T]) ((handle[T], *T) | done)
lora 
use pool;

type node = struct { name: str, parent: pool::handle[node] }

fn depth(nodes: *pool::pool[node], h: pool::handle[node]) int = {
	let d = 0;
	let at = h;
	for (true) match (pool::get(nodes, at)) {
		null => break,
		let n: *node => {
			d += 1;
			at = n.parent;
		},
	}
	return d;
}

export fn main() void = {
	let nodes = pool::new::[node]();
	let root = pool::put(&nodes, node { name = "root", ... })!;
	let leaf = pool::put(&nodes, node { name = "leaf", parent = root })!;
	assert(depth(&nodes, leaf) == 2);
	pool::remove(&nodes, root);              // the leaf's parent link is stale
	assert(depth(&nodes, leaf) == 1);
}
  • Owners: a pool can hold them. Removing a value, clearing the pool or dropping it drops what it holds; take gives one back to be owned.
  • Pointers from get view the pool: a put may move the slots, so a pointer from before it can't be used after it (L0609).
  • Handles of another pool find nothing, even of the same type; the zero handle, pool::handle::[T] { ... }, stands for none.
  • Sealed: a pool's fields are this module's alone. Its zero value, pool::pool::[T] { ... }, is an empty pool, as new gives.
  • Cost: put, get, take and remove are constant time, and a removed value's slot is used again. A slot is retired, not reused, once its generation would run out.

thread — OS threads, mutexes, condition variables, atomics

lora 
type thread = struct { … }
fn spawn(body: closure() void) (thread | nomem)   // takes only what it owns
	fn spawn_with[T](v: T, body: closure(v: T) void) (thread | nomem) // gives it v
	fn detach(t: thread) void
	fn join(t: thread) void
	fn join_all(ts: *^[]thread) void          // each, leaving ts empty

	type mutex = struct { … }
fn mutex_init(m: *mutex) void
	fn mutex_finish(m: *mutex) void
	fn lock(m: *mutex) void
	fn unlock(m: *mutex) void

	type cond = struct { … }
fn cond_init(c: *cond) void
	fn cond_finish(c: *cond) void
	fn wait(c: *cond, m: *mutex) void
	fn signal(c: *cond) void
	fn broadcast(c: *cond) void

	type atomic = struct { … }              // atomic { ... } holds 0
fn new_atomic(v: u64) atomic
	fn add(a: *atomic, n: u64) u64          // returns the previous value
	fn load(a: *atomic) u64
	fn store(a: *atomic, v: u64) void
	fn cas(a: *atomic, expected: u64, desired: u64) bool

	fn new_mutex() mutex                    // ready to use, as a global's value too

	type shared[T] = struct { … }
fn new_shared[T](v: T) shared[T]         // v, guarded by a lock
	fn with[T](s: *shared[T], body: closure(v: *T) void) void // holds the lock
	fn lock_shared[T](s: *const shared[T]) *T   // locks it, through a read-only path too
	fn unlock_shared[T](s: *const shared[T]) void

Threads are pthreads. A thread runs a closure, which copies what it captures, so give it pointers to shared data and make that data thread-safe: an atomic, a shared[T], or data changed only between lock and unlock. The compiler reports threads changing other shared data (L0700, see "Data races" in the language reference). The atomics are sequentially consistent (ldaddal/casal on arm64, lock xadd/cmpxchg on x86_64).

A thread is joined or detached once: it is moved, never copied, and one dropped with neither is detached, to finish on its own. Keep several in a ^[]thread and join_all them. The types here are @sealed: an atomic's value is reached by its functions, a shared value through its lock. Each zero value is ready to use: mutex { ... } and cond { ... }, an atomic { ... } holding 0, and thread { ... }, no thread, which join and detach leave alone.

scratch — memory for a piece of work

Scratch memory is room for what a piece of work needs only while it runs, given back all at once when it ends. Each coroutine has its own scratch region, and each thread one for code outside coroutines; it sizes itself and keeps its pages, so taking scratch costs one pointer move and no lock.

lora 
type frame = struct { … }
fn with[R](body: *closure(s: *frame) R) R      // gives back all it took
fn make[T](s: *frame, n: usize) ([]T | nomem)  // zeroed
fn new[T](s: *frame, v: T) (*T | nomem)
fn copy(s: *frame, text: str) (str | nomem)
fn used(s: *frame) usize
lora 
use scratch;
use strings;

fn longest(words: []str) usize = scratch::with(fn(s: *scratch::frame) usize = {
	// upper-cased copies, needed only to measure them
	let n = 0z;
	for (let w .. words) {
		let buf = scratch::make::[u8](s, len(w))!;
		for (let i = 0z; i < len(w); i += 1) buf[i] = strings::to_bytes(w)[i] & 0xdf;
		if (len(buf) > n) n = len(buf);
	}
	return n;
});

export fn main() void = assert(longest(["ada", "lovelace"]) == 8);
  • Nesting: with marks where the scratch region is and goes back to the mark when its body returns, so an inner with gives back only what it took.
  • Coroutines: a coroutine keeps its scratch wherever it runs, so its body may wait (a channel, a socket, coro::sleep) while others use theirs.
  • Checked: what the body takes views its frame. Returning it from the body (@borrows(R) is refused), storing it in a global, or keeping it through a captured pointer is an error.

coro — coroutines (green threads), channels, select, non-blocking I/O

Coroutines are lightweight, cooperative tasks, not OS threads. run starts a worker thread per processor and runs coroutines on them many-to-many. Each worker hosts any number of coroutines, taking turns, and a coroutine can move to another worker whenever it resumes. run_on(1) keeps everything on one thread (many-to-one).

A coroutine runs until it reaches a suspension point, which frees its thread for other coroutines:

Suspension point
yield_now()let other ready coroutines go first
sleep(ms)a delay, on a kqueue timer
read, write, wait_readable, wait_writable (and _within a time), net's socketsnon-blocking I/O, parked on kqueue
send, recv, selectchannels
group_waitwaiting for other coroutines
blocking(fn)a blocking call, run on a helper thread meanwhile

Work is started by @all, @first and @scope (with @go), which wait for it (see Concurrency in language.md), or detached:

lora 
// structured: cancelled children's waits end at once
type cancelled = !void "cancelled"
type timed_out = !struct { within: u64 }            // within = ms ran out
fn check() (void | cancelled)                      // coro::check()?;
fn is_cancelled() bool
fn alone() bool                                   // the last of its scope's coroutines, the scope's code waiting

// timers: sleeping in and out of coroutines, ticking, and running later
fn sleep_for(d: time::duration) void              // others run meanwhile; cancelling ends it
fn sleep_until(at: time::instant) void
type ticker = struct { ... }
fn new_ticker(period: time::duration) ticker      // its first tick a period from now
fn tick(t: *ticker) time::instant                 // waits for the next; missed ones are dropped
fn reset_ticker(t: *ticker, period: time::duration) void
fn run_after(d: time::duration, f: closure() void) (detached | nomem)   // cancel stops it
fn run_after_with[T](d: time::duration, v: T, f: *fn(v: T) void) (detached | nomem)

// serial values: one coroutine at a time, which may not wait meanwhile
type serial[T] = struct { … }
fn serial_new[T](v: T) serial[T]
fn with[T, R](s: *serial[T], f: *closure(v: *T) R) R

// detached: nothing waits for them, so they take only what they own
type detached = struct { id: u64 }                 // never reused
fn detach(body: closure() void) (detached | nomem)
fn detach_sized(stack: usize, body: closure() void) (detached | nomem)
fn detach_with[T](v: T, body: closure(v: T) void) (detached | nomem)
fn detach_with_sized[T](stack: usize, v: T, body: closure(v: T) void) (detached | nomem)
fn cancel(d: detached) bool                       // false: it had finished
fn running(d: detached) bool

// priority: children start with their parent's; waiting raises theirs
type priority = enum u8 { low, normal, high }
fn priority_now() priority
fn set_priority(p: priority) void

// task-local values, seen by the coroutine and its children
type local[T] = struct { name: str }
fn bind[T, R](key: *local[T], v: T, body: *closure() R) R
fn lookup[T](key: *local[T]) (T | void)
fn run() void                                     // a worker per processor
fn run_on(n: usize) void
fn yield_now() void
fn sleep(ms: u64) void
fn blocking(body: closure() void) void
fn cpus() usize
fn worker_id() int                                // -1 outside of run
fn workers() usize

// non-blocking I/O
fn read(fd: int, buf: []u8) (usize | coro::error)
fn write(fd: int, buf: []u8) (void | coro::error)
fn nonblocking(fd: int) void
fn wait_readable(fd: int) void
fn wait_writable(fd: int) void
fn wait_readable_within(fd: int, ms: u64) bool        // false: the time ran out
fn wait_writable_within(fd: int, ms: u64) bool

// channels: buffered, or unbuffered with capacity 0 (send waits for a receiver);
// values that own memory are moved through them: a send gives one away, a
// receive owns it, and what is left in a channel is dropped with it
// (send_case takes no such value: use send)
type chan[T] = struct { … }
fn chan_new[T](capacity: usize) chan[T]         // capacity * size_of(T) bytes must be countable
fn chan_finish[T](c: *chan[T]) void
fn send[T](c: *chan[T], v: T) (void | done)        // done: closed
fn recv[T](c: *chan[T]) (T | done)
fn close[T](c: *chan[T]) void

// select over channels of any types; try_select is select with a default
type case = struct { … }
fn recv_case[T](c: *chan[T], out: *T) case
fn send_case[T](c: *chan[T], v: *T) case
fn select(cases: []case) (usize, bool)             // case index, and false if closed
fn try_select(cases: []case) ((usize, bool) | void)

// wait groups
type group = struct { … }
fn group_new() group
fn group_add(g: *group, n: usize) void
fn group_done(g: *group) void
fn group_wait(g: *group) void

Channels, select cases, groups, scopes and serial values are @sealed: the scheduler trusts their fields, so only this module reads and writes them. A case is made by recv_case or send_case; a channel's zero value, chan::[T] { ... }, is an unbuffered one, and a group's, a scope's and a serial value's are ready to use, as their _new functions give.

lora 
let pages = @all(max = 8) for (let u .. urls) fetch(u);
@scope {
	@go for (true) {
		let v = 0, quit = false;
		match coro::select([
			coro::recv_case(&results, &v),
			coro::recv_case(&stop, &quit),
		]) {
			(0, true) => handle(v),
			_ => break, // stopped, or cancelled: (len(cases), false)
		}
	}
}?;

Scheduling. Each worker has its own run queue and runs from it first. A coroutine readied on a worker (spawned, woken, yielding) goes on that worker's queue. Workers check a global queue every 61 turns and right after a yield, and steal half of another worker's queue when they run dry, which balances load and moves coroutines between threads. One worker at a time waits on kqueue. When a coroutine suspends, its worker carries out the suspension (requeueing it, releasing a channel lock, registering an event) only after the coroutine's registers are saved, so other threads can never resume it too early. 1000 coroutines × 1000 yields take 0.19s on 8 workers.

Stacks. Each coroutine has a fixed 256 KiB stack (detach_sized for more) with a guard page. Only touched pages use memory. Stacks do not grow: overflowing one faults on the guard page. The compiler reports a coroutine or thread whose code needs more stack than it gets as an error, and warns when it calls a recursive function (see "Stack overflow check" in tooling.md).

Rules. Code in coroutines on different workers runs in parallel, so protect shared data with thread::mutex, atomics or channels. If every remaining coroutine is waiting on a channel or group, run aborts with a deadlock message. λexamples/coro_echo.lora is a TCP echo server with a coroutine per connection.

rc — shared ownership

lora 
type rc[T];     // a shared owner of a T
type weak[T];   // a pointer to it that does not keep it alive

fn new[T](v: T) (rc[T] | nomem)          // v moves in
	fn share[T](r: *rc[T]) rc[T]             // another owner
	fn get[T](r: *rc[T]) *T                  // a borrow of the value
	fn count[T](r: *rc[T]) usize
	fn downgrade[T](r: *rc[T]) weak[T]
	fn upgrade[T](w: *weak[T]) (rc[T] | void) // an owner, while the value lives

Unique owners (^T) and borrows are Lora's default; rc is for data that genuinely needs several owners. Each rc drops its share when its owner ends; the last one drops the value. weak breaks cycles. For one thread.

new refuses a type that could own itself through rc, which would never be freed: a link back is a weak. See the language reference's Ownership.

arc — shared ownership across threads

lora 
type arc[T];
fn new[T](v: T) (arc[T] | nomem)
	fn share[T](a: *arc[T]) arc[T]
	fn get[T](a: *arc[T]) *T
	fn count[T](a: *arc[T]) usize

rc with atomic counts. The value is shared, not locked: guard changes with thread::mutex.

unit — what a function reports

Put unit::error in a function's result type, and a false requires or ensures is returned instead of stopping the program. See the language reference's Unit functions.

lora 
type precondition_failed = !struct { function: str, predicate: str, message: str };
type postcondition_failed = !struct { function: str, predicate: str, message: str };
type expectation_failed = !struct { function: str, predicate: str, last: str, waited_ms: u64 };
type error = !(precondition_failed | postcondition_failed | expectation_failed);

predicate is the condition as written, and message is the one written with it, or "". A failure prints as withdraw requires cents > 0: the amount must be positive, or without a message, withdraw requires cents > 0.

@expect fails with expectation_failed. Its predicate is what the last attempt failed to see: the condition of an assert, the type of an as, or no error for a ?. Its last is what that attempt saw: the message and the values compared, what the as found, or the error's message. It prints as open: expected d.id == id, after 2000 ms: not loaded: d.id is 2, id is 1.

last has nothing to free, because it is kept in one of 32 fixed places, and is cut at about 500 bytes. After 32 more @expects have timed out, in any thread, its place is used again, so copy it with strings::clone to keep it for longer.

expanse — memory that grows in place

A region reserves a large range of address space up front, far more than it will ever need, without committing it: that costs next to nothing. As it fills, it commits more pages at the end of the range, so it grows without moving: a pointer into it stays good until the region is reset or finished, and growing never copies.

expanse::auto() chooses no size: it reserves nothing until something is put in it, then AUTO (64 MiB) of address space, which takes no memory until pages are used. When that fills it reserves another range, twice as large (or as large as one thing asked for), and goes on there: what it holds never moves, and thousands of auto regions can be in use at once. A region owned by a block, a coroutine's body or a request lives as long as it does, with no size to guess:

lora 
use expanse;

fn names(n: int) usize = {
	let r = expanse::auto();               // freed when the function ends
	let total = 0z;
	for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 1) {
		let s = expanse::copy(&r, "a name")!;
		total += len(s);
	}
	return total;
}

export fn main() void = assert(names(1000) == 6000);

What a region holds is a view of it, checked as any view is: it can't be stored where it outlives the region, nor used after reset, rewind, shrink or finish (L0608, L0609). Taking more from a region ends nothing taken before. Its fields are this module's alone (@sealed): its zero value, region { ... }, which blank tells, holds nothing, and anything asked of it fails as full. A struct can hold a region with views of what it holds, as json::document does: moving the region moves no memory.

lora 
def KIB, MIB, GIB, TIB: usize

type region = struct { … }
type mark = struct { … }
type full = !struct { wanted: usize, left: usize, reserved: usize }
type uncommitted = !struct { wanted: usize }

fn reserve(bytes: usize) (region | nomem)        // address space, no memory
fn auto() region                                 // sizes itself: nothing until used
fn finish(r: *region) void                       // give it all back

fn new[T](r: *region, v: T) (*T | full | uncommitted)
fn make[T](r: *region, n: usize) ([]T | full | uncommitted)  // zeroed
fn copy(r: *region, s: str) (str | full | uncommitted)
fn take(r: *region, bytes: usize, alignment: usize)
	(*opaque | full | uncommitted)                // not cleared

fn here(r: *const region) mark
fn rewind(r: *region, m: mark) void              // back to a mark, in any range
fn reset(r: *region) void                        // empty; keeps the pages
fn reset_poisoned(r: *region) void               // and overwrites them
fn shrink(r: *region) (void | uncommitted)       // gives pages and ranges back

fn used(r: *const region) usize
fn committed(r: *const region) usize
fn reserved(r: *const region) usize
fn contains(r: *const region, p: *const opaque) bool
fn blank(r: *const region) bool                  // its zero value, region { ... }

type array[T] = struct { … }
fn array_new[T](capacity: usize) (array[T] | nomem)
fn array_finish[T](a: *array[T]) void
fn push[T](a: *array[T], v: T) (*T | full | uncommitted)  // never moves
fn pop[T](a: *array[T]) (T | void)
fn items[T](a: *array[T]) []T
fn capacity[T](a: *const array[T]) usize
fn array_clear[T](a: *array[T]) void
lora 
use expanse;

type node = struct { value: int, next: nullable *node }

export fn main() void = {
	let r = expanse::reserve(64 * expanse::GIB)!;   // takes no memory yet
	defer expanse::finish(&r);
	let first = expanse::new(&r, node { value = 1, next = null })!;
	for (let i = 2; i <= 100000; i += 1) {
		expanse::new(&r, node { value = i, next = null })!;
	}
	assert(first.value == 1);                       // first never moved

	let a = expanse::array_new::[int](1000000000)!; // room for 10^9
	defer expanse::array_finish(&a);
	let p = expanse::push(&a, 7)!;
	for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i += 1) expanse::push(&a, i)!;
	assert(*p == 7 && len(expanse::items(&a)) == 100001);
}

Sizes. KIB, MIB, GIB and TIB are a kibibyte, a mebibyte, a gibibyte and a tebibyte in bytes (1024, 1024², 1024³, 1024⁴), the units reserve is given its size in: expanse::reserve(64 * expanse::GIB) rather than 68719476736. AUTO, the address space an auto region reserves when it is first used, is 64 MIB; each range after is twice the last, up to a TIB at a time. A region commits pages at least one MIB at a time. KIB suits a small region: expanse::reserve(64 * expanse::KIB).

When to use one. For data that lives and dies together: a request, a frame, a parse tree, a compiler pass. Measured on an M-series Mac, for ten million small nodes:

makefreetotal
alloc and free165 ms115 ms280 ms
expanse::new and finish85 ms2 ms87 ms

For a large growing array, push is about 20% slower than append, which macOS can often grow in place too: use array when something points into it, since a slice's append may move every element. Five thousand auto regions in use at once take 30 ms to make, and memory only for the pages they use.

make clears only memory that may hold old values, after rewind or reset: fresh pages are zero already, so a large make on a new region touches nothing (50 of 256 MiB each take 4 ms, where clearing them took 7 s), and copy writes each byte once.

How it works. reserve maps the range with no access (mmap with PROT_NONE), and committing makes the next pages usable (mprotect), so touching memory past what is committed faults instead of corrupting anything. Page size comes from the system (16 KiB on Apple Silicon). Commits grow with the region, so they are rare. shrink replaces pages with fresh inaccessible ones, which gives them back. An auto region's ranges each start with a few bytes that link them; rewind and reset keep the later ranges, so filling the region again costs no system call, and shrink gives them back.

Rules.

  • Choose a reservation far bigger than you expect to need: it is the most the region can ever hold (full), and costs next to nothing.
  • Nothing in a region is freed alone: never free a pointer from one.
  • reset, rewind and finish end what they give back, and the compiler does not follow pointers past them. reset_poisoned makes a stale pointer read 0xcc at once, for finding such bugs.
  • Store plain data: owners (^T) put in a region are not dropped.
  • A region is for one thread at a time; the compiler reports threads changing one they share (L0700).
  • The compiler reports pointers to locals stored in a region (L0104).

new, make and push refuse a type that owns memory: a region frees everything at once, and drops nothing.

allocator — where memory comes from

For code that is given where its memory comes from: one interface, allocator::allocator, and allocators behind it. These are the system heap; a region (from_region); a fixed buffer, which hands out its memory in order, and a lock-free one for threads; a fixed buffer that falls back to another allocator when it is full (stack_fallback); a slab of same-size slots; a free list with size classes; a ring, for memory given back in the order it was taken; a lock around another allocator (thread_safe); and set_global, which routes alloc, free and append through one. The allocators guide says when to use each, with examples.

lora 
use allocator;

export fn main() void = {
	let fb = allocator::fixed_buffer_owned(4096)!;  // 4096 bytes of its own
	let a: allocator::allocator = &fb;
	let xs = allocator::make::[u32](a, 64)!;        // views a, so fb
	xs[63] = 7;
	let name = allocator::copy_str(a, "ada")!;
	assert(name == "ada" && xs[63] == 7);
	assert(allocator::fixed_buffer_used(&fb) >= 64 * 4 + 3);
	allocator::fixed_buffer_reset(&fb);              // xs and name end here
	assert(allocator::fixed_buffer_used(&fb) == 0);
}

What create, make and copy_str give is a view of the allocator, checked as any view is: it can't outlive the allocator, nor the buffer the allocator hands out (L0608). Resetting or rewinding an allocator ends what it gave (L0609). A fixed buffer's mark and rewind give back everything taken since the mark, as a region's do.

Buffers. The fixed buffer, atomic fixed buffer, stack fallback, free list and ring each take their memory one of two ways. X_owned(n) gives them n zeroed bytes of their own, freed when they are dropped: nothing else can write those bytes, so it is safe. X_new(buf) lends them a buffer you have, as an array on the stack, so that nothing is allocated: it is unsafe, as what they hand out lives in buf, and nothing else may write buf while any of it is in use. These allocators are moved, never copied: two copies would hand out the same bytes.

Sealed. The allocator types are @sealed: only this module reads and writes their fields. Each one's zero value, T { ... }, holds nothing, and anything asked of it fails with nomem.

Unsafe. Giving memory back one piece at a time is unsafe: destroy, free_slice, free_str, grow and resize_slice, slab_free, and the interface's resize_bytes, realloc_bytes and free_bytes, which are @unsafe methods. The caller makes sure the memory came from that allocator, at that size and alignment, and that nothing uses it after (L0800). For memory freed all at once, by a reset, nothing is unsafe.

Threads. system and atomic_fixed_buffer guard themselves, and thread_safe puts a lock around another allocator: they are @synchronised, so @go children may share a pointer to one, and make the interface in the child. An interface value itself can't be shared: what it points to may be of any type. thread_safe_new is unsafe, as every use of the allocator it wraps must go through its lock, and atomic_fixed_buffer_reset is unsafe, as the compiler can't see what other threads still hold.

lora 
type allocator = interface {
	fn alloc_bytes(n: usize, alignment: usize) (*opaque | nomem);
	@unsafe fn resize_bytes(p: *opaque, old_n: usize, new_n: usize, alignment: usize) bool;
	@unsafe fn realloc_bytes(p: *opaque, old_n: usize, new_n: usize, alignment: usize) (*opaque | nomem);
	@unsafe fn free_bytes(p: *opaque, n: usize, alignment: usize) void;
}

fn create[T](a: allocator, v: T) (*T | nomem)          // views a
fn make[T](a: allocator, n: usize) ([]T | nomem)       // zeroed; views a
fn copy_str(a: allocator, s: str) (str | nomem)        // views a
@unsafe fn destroy[T](a: allocator, p: *T) void
@unsafe fn free_slice[T](a: allocator, s: []T) void
@unsafe fn free_str(a: allocator, s: str) void
@unsafe fn grow[T](a: allocator, s: []T, n: usize) ([]T | nomem)
@unsafe fn resize_slice[T](a: allocator, s: []T, n: usize) ([]T | void)

fn system_allocator() allocator                         // shared by threads
fn from_region(r: *expanse::region) region_allocator

fn fixed_buffer_owned(n: usize) (fixed_buffer | nomem)
@unsafe fn fixed_buffer_new(buf: []u8) fixed_buffer     // views buf
fn fixed_buffer_used(fb: *const fixed_buffer) usize
fn fixed_buffer_remaining(fb: *const fixed_buffer) usize
fn fixed_buffer_mark(fb: *const fixed_buffer) fixed_mark
fn fixed_buffer_rewind(fb: *fixed_buffer, m: fixed_mark) void
fn fixed_buffer_reset(fb: *fixed_buffer) void

fn atomic_fixed_buffer_owned(n: usize) (atomic_fixed_buffer | nomem)
@unsafe fn atomic_fixed_buffer_new(buf: []u8) atomic_fixed_buffer
fn atomic_fixed_buffer_used(af: *const atomic_fixed_buffer) usize
@unsafe fn atomic_fixed_buffer_reset(af: *atomic_fixed_buffer) void

fn stack_fallback_owned(n: usize, fallback: allocator) (stack_fallback | nomem)
@unsafe fn stack_fallback_new(buf: []u8, fallback: allocator) stack_fallback
fn stack_fallback_reset(sf: *stack_fallback) void

fn slab_new(backing: allocator, slot_size: usize, slot_align: usize, slots_per_chunk: usize) slab
fn slab_alloc(s: *slab) (*opaque | nomem)               // views s
@unsafe fn slab_free(s: *slab, p: *opaque) void
fn slab_live(s: *const slab) usize
fn slab_reset(s: *slab) void
fn slab_finish(s: *slab) void

fn free_list_owned(n: usize) (free_list | nomem)
@unsafe fn free_list_new(buf: []u8) free_list
fn free_list_used(fl: *const free_list) usize
fn free_list_reset(fl: *free_list) void

fn ring_owned(n: usize) (ring | nomem)
@unsafe fn ring_new(buf: []u8) ring
fn ring_live(rg: *const ring) usize
fn ring_reset(rg: *ring) void

@unsafe fn thread_safe_new(inner: allocator) thread_safe
@unsafe fn set_global(a: *allocator) void
@unsafe fn reset_global() void

A fixed buffer takes memory from its buffer in order, each piece aligned as asked, and fails with nomem when the buffer is used up: it never asks the system for more. Giving back the last piece taken, or growing it, works where it is; anything else waits for rewind or reset. For one piece of work, scratch::with needs no buffer and never runs out; for typed values that never move, expanse::reserve.

Which to use. The default alloc and growing ^[]T for most things; scratch for what a piece of work needs only while it runs; expanse for many values that live and die together; pool for values that refer to each other. Use an allocator from this module when code must be told where its memory comes from: a fixed buffer with a hard limit, a slab for many values of one size, or a ring for a queue of messages.

config — settings from the environment

Tags say where each field of a struct comes from, and load reads them all. It expands into one read per field while compiling.

lora 
type field = struct {
	key: str = "",        // the name in errors
	env: str = "",        // the environment variable
	default: (void | int | bool | str) = void,
	skip: bool = false,
}
type error = !struct { key: str, env: str, why: str }
fn load[T]() (T | error | nomem)
lora 
use config;

type server = struct {
	@config("port", env = "PORT", default = 8080) port: int,
	@config("host", env = "HOST", default = "127.0.0.1") host: str,
	@config("db_url", env = "DB_URL") db_url: str,  // must be set
	@config("name", env = "NAME") name: ?str,       // void if it is not set
}

export fn main() (void | config::error | nomem) = {
	let s = config::load::[server]()?;
}
text 
error: config: db_url: not set in DB_URL

A field can be int, bool, str, or ? of one, and each needs a tag. If its variable is not set, a field with a default takes it, a ? field is void, and any other field is an error from load. The tags are checked while compiling, even if load is never called: a field nothing can set, a default of the wrong type, and two fields with one key are errors. Settings come from the environment the program started with (os::start_env), which os::setenv doesn't change. str fields are views of it or of the tag, and last as long as the program.

json — JSON text, documents and types

Strict by default, as RFC 7493 asks of RFC 8259 JSON: text must be valid UTF-8, an object must not repeat a name, NaN and infinity have no form, and a text is one value. options relaxes or extends each of these.

lora 
type options = struct {
	reject_unknown: bool = false,     // a member no field takes is an error
	ignore_case: bool = false,        // names match ignoring case, - and _
	allow_duplicates: bool = false,   // a repeated name: the last one wins
	allow_invalid_utf8: bool = false, // bad bytes read and written as U+FFFD
	max_depth: usize = 128,           // arrays and objects nested deeper: an error
	numbers_as_strings: bool = false, // numbers written as "42", and read so
	indent: str = "",                 // "" for one line; else one item a line
	space_after_comma: bool = false,
	sorted: bool = false,             // members by name: the same bytes each time
	escape_html: bool = false,        // <, > and & escaped
	empty_as_null: bool = false,      // empty slices written as null
	omit_zero: bool = false,          // every field as if tagged omit_zero
}

Writing refuses a value nested deeper than json::WRITE_DEPTH (128) with an error, rather than running out of stack: a document read with a larger max_depth can hold one.

Errors

Each says where: the byte, and the JSON pointer (RFC 6901) to the value. Errors own and view nothing, so they outlive the text.

ErrorMessage
invalidinvalid JSON at byte 14 (/users/2): expected ',' or ']'
mismatchcannot read int from JSON at byte 30 (/age): expected an integer
missinguser.email is missing from the JSON object at byte 0
unknownuser has no field for the JSON member at byte 41 (/nickname)

json::path(&e.at) is the pointer, e.at.pos the byte; invalid's why is a reason, with reason_text.

Tokens

lora 
type token = (void | bool | str | number | delim);  // void is null
type number = struct { text: str }                  // as written: exact
fn as_i64(n: number) (i64 | void)      // also as_u64, as_f64, as_f32
fn new_reader(text: str, opts: options = ...) reader
	fn stream_reader(r: io::reader, opts: options = ...) reader  // read as it comes
	fn next(r: *reader) (token | done | invalid | io::failure)
	fn peek(r: *reader) (kind | done | ...)        // without reading it
	fn skip(r: *reader) (void | done | ...)        // all of the next value
	fn read_raw(r: *reader) (str | done | ...)     // the next value's text
	fn here(r: *reader) place      // the next token: its byte and pointer
	fn last(r: *reader) place      // the token just read
	fn depth(r: *reader) usize
fn new_writer(out: *^[]u8, opts: options = ...) writer
	fn stream_writer(w: io::writer, opts: options = ...) writer  // and flush
	fn put(w: *writer, t: token) (void | invalid | io::failure)
	fn put_int(w, i64), put_uint(w, u64), put_float(w, f64), put_raw(w, str), put_value(w, value)

A reader checks what it reads and a writer what it writes, at once: a string in an object is a member's name, and a name given twice is an error. A string or number a reader gives is good until its next call. A reader of a file reads a stream of values, one after another, as they are asked for.

Numbers are written in the shortest form that reads back as the same number (1, 0.1, 1e+21), and read exactly: an integer that does not fit its type is an error, never a wrapped or rounded number.

Text as text

lora 
type raw = str;                           // JSON text, kept as written
fn valid(text: str, opts: options = ...) bool
fn format(text: str, opts: options = ...) (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn compact(text: str) (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn indent(text: str, by: str = "\t") (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn canonical(text: str) (^str | invalid | nomem)   // RFC 8785, to sign or hash

Documents

lora 
type value = (str | f64 | bool | []value | []member | void);  // void = null
type member = struct { key: str, val: value }
type document = struct { root: value, mem: expanse::region }
fn parse(input: str, opts: options = ...) (document | invalid | nomem)
	fn finish(d: *document) void            // frees it now, rather than when dropped
	fn to_str(v: value, opts: options = ...) (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn get(v: value, key: str) (value | void)
	fn at(v: value, pointer: str) (value | void)   // RFC 6901: "/users/0/name"

A document keeps its values in a region of its own: they are views into it, good while it lives, and dropping it frees them all at once. Objects keep their members' order, unless written sorted.

Types

lora 
type field = struct {
	name: str = "",
	omit_empty: bool = false,  // left out when null, "", [] or {}
	omit_zero: bool = false,   // left out when its type's zero
	skip: bool = false,        // never written or read
	string: bool = false,      // a number written as a string
	ignore_case: bool = false, // its name matched ignoring case, - and _
	strict_case: bool = false, // its name matched exactly, whatever the options
	format: str = "",          // base64url, unix_ms, ...: see below
	inline: bool = false,      // a struct whose fields are this object's
	unknown: bool = false,     // a json::value of the members no field takes
}
fn marshal[T](v: *const T, opts: options = ...) (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn marshal_to[T](w: *writer, v: *const T) (void | invalid | io::failure)
	fn unmarshal[T](r: *expanse::region, input: str, opts: options = ...)
	(T | invalid | mismatch | missing | unknown | expanse::full | expanse::uncommitted | nomem)
	fn unmarshal_from[T](r: *expanse::region, rd: *reader) (T | done | ...)  // one value of a stream

marshal and unmarshal expand into code for each type while compiling, with no reflection at run time: a type with no JSON form is a compile error. Every integer and float type (range-checked when read), bool, str, enums (by their members' names), optionals, arrays, slices, structs, map::map[str, V] (an object), []u8 (base64), time::datetime (RFC 3339), value and raw have a form.

A type of your own takes a form of its own by implementing encoder and decoder, whose methods take it as *const T and *T:

lora 
type encoder = interface { fn encode_json(w: *writer) (void | invalid | io::failure); }
type decoder = interface { fn decode_json(rd: *reader, r: *expanse::region) (void | ...); }

The tag's other options:

  • format: base64 (the default), base64url, base64raw or base64url_raw for a []u8; rfc3339 (the default), unix_ms or unix for a time::datetime.
  • inline: a struct whose fields are this object's, as if they were its own.
  • unknown: a json::value that takes the members no field takes, and writes them back in their place.
lora 
use expanse;
use json;

type user = struct {
	@json("id") id: int,
	@json("display_name") name: str,
	@json("email", omit_empty) email: str,   // left out when empty
	@json(skip) pw_hash: str,                // never read or written
	tags: []str,                             // no tag: its own name
}

export fn main() void = {
	let u = user { id = 1, name = "ada", email = "", pw_hash = "x", tags = [] }
	let text = json::marshal(&u)!;
	let r = expanse::reserve(expanse::GIB)!;
	defer expanse::finish(&r);
	let back = json::unmarshal::[user](&r, text)!;
	assert(back.name == "ada");
}

unmarshal reads tokens straight into the value, with no tree between, and copies strings and slices into the region, where they live until it is reset. A field absent from the text is an error (missing) unless it is skip, optional, omit_empty or omit_zero; a member with no field is skipped, or an error with reject_unknown.

encoding — text and binary forms types share

encodings.md shows every encoding module with a working example; λexamples/encodings.lora, λpem_asn1.lora, λcsv.lora, λxml.lora and λpack.lora are longer programs.

lora 
type text_encoder = interface { fn encode_text(out: *^[]u8) (void | nomem); }
type text_decoder = interface { fn decode_text(text: str) (void | invalid | nomem); }
type binary_encoder = interface { fn encode_binary(out: *^[]u8) (void | nomem); }
type binary_decoder = interface { fn decode_binary(data: []const u8) (void | invalid | nomem); }
type invalid = !struct { ... }     // why the input is not the form
fn refuse(why: str) invalid;  fn reason(e: *const invalid) str

A type with a text form of its own implements text_encoder (its method takes it as *const T) and text_decoder, and json writes and reads it as a string; xml, csv and the others will too. uuid::uuid and time::datetime do. A decoder copies what it keeps of its input.

hex — hexadecimal

Example: λexamples/encodings.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
fn encode(b: []const u8, upper: bool = false) (^str | nomem)
	fn encode_into(b: []const u8, out: []u8, upper: bool = false) []u8
	fn append_encode(out: *^[]u8, b: []const u8, upper: bool = false) (void | nomem)
fn decode(text: str) (^[]u8 | invalid | odd_length | nomem)   // either case
	fn decode_into(text: str, out: []u8) ([]u8 | invalid | odd_length)
	fn append_decode(out: *^[]u8, text: str) (void | invalid | odd_length | nomem)
	fn value(c: u8) (u8 | void)                   // one digit's value
fn encoded_len(n: usize) usize;  fn decoded_len(n: usize) usize
fn dump(b: []const u8) (^str | nomem)           // as hexdump -C writes it
	fn new_dumper(out: *^[]u8) dumper;  fn dump_write(d, b);  fn dump_close(d)

invalid says which byte is not a digit, and where. dump writes an offset, sixteen bytes in hex, and the printable ones; a dumper does the same for bytes as they come.

base64, base32, ascii85 — bytes as text

Example: λexamples/encodings.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
// base64: std, url (- and _), raw_std, raw_url (no padding)
fn encode(b: []const u8) (^str | nomem);  fn encode_with(c: coding, b: []const u8)
	fn encode_into_with(c, b, out: []u8) []u8;  fn append_encode_with(c, out: *^[]u8, b)
	fn decode(text: str) (^[]u8 | invalid | nomem);  fn decode_with(c, text)
	fn decode_into_with(c, text, out: []u8) ([]u8 | invalid)
	fn append_decode_with(c, out: *^[]u8, text: str, lines: bool = false)  // lines skips \r \n
	fn new_encoder(c, out: *^[]u8) encoder;  fn encoder_write(e, b);  fn encoder_close(e)
	fn new_decoder(c, out: *^[]u8) decoder;  fn decoder_write(d, text);  fn decoder_close(d)
// base32: std (A-Z 2-7), hex (0-9 A-V, sorts as the bytes do), raw_std, raw_hex
	the same functions as base64
// ascii85: four bytes as five characters ! to u, four zero bytes as z
fn encode, encode_into, append_encode, decode, decode_into, append_decode
	fn max_encoded_len(n: usize) usize;  fn max_decoded_len(n: usize) usize
	new_encoder, encoder_write, encoder_close, new_decoder, decoder_write, decoder_close

base64 and base32 decode strictly: a character outside the alphabet, padding where it can't be, or unused low bits that aren't zero is invalid, with the byte where, so that every value has one encoding. ascii85 skips whitespace, and reads z only between groups. An encoder or decoder works on bytes or text as they come, a group at a time, and gives what one call on the whole would.

binary — byte orders, varints and fixed layouts

Example: λexamples/encodings.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
fn be16(b: []const u8) u16      // also be32, be64, le16, le32, le64
	fn put_be16(b: []u8, v: u16) void         // and put_le..., for every size
	fn append_be16(out: *^[]u8, v: u16) (void | nomem)   // and append_le...
fn put_uvarint(b: []u8, v: u64) usize;  fn append_uvarint(out: *^[]u8, v: u64)
	fn uvarint(b: []const u8) ((u64, usize) | bad_varint)
	fn put_varint, append_varint, varint      // zigzag, for signed integers
type order = enum { big, little }
fn fixed_size[T]() usize                  // a record's bytes, with no padding
	fn write[T](o: order, out: *^[]u8, v: *const T) (void | nomem)
	fn read[T](o: order, b: []const u8, out: *T) (usize | short | invalid)

A varint takes seven bits a byte, least significant first; MAX_VARINT64 is the most it takes. write and read lay a record out field by field, with no padding, in the byte order given: integers, floats, bools, enums, and arrays and structs of them. The code for each type is made while compiling. read checks that bools are 0 or 1 and enums one of their members.

csv — comma-separated values

Example: λexamples/csv.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
type options = struct {
	comma: u8 = ',', comment: u8 = 0, lazy_quotes: bool = false,
	trim_leading_space: bool = false,
	fields: int = 0,     // per record: 0 as many as the first, -1 any
	crlf: bool = false,  // records written ending \r\n
	header: bool = true, // marshal and unmarshal: the first record names columns
}
fn new_reader(text: str, opts = options { ... }) reader;  fn stream_reader(r: io::reader, opts)
	fn read(r: *reader) ([]str | done | invalid | io::failure)  // good until the next read
	fn read_all(r, m: *expanse::region) ([][]str | ...)
	fn field_pos(r, i: usize) (usize, usize);  fn record_line(r) usize
fn new_writer(out: *^[]u8, opts) writer;  fn stream_writer(w: io::writer, opts) writer
	fn write(w, fields: []const str);  fn write_field(w, s: str);  fn end_record(w);  fn flush(w)
fn unmarshal[T](m: *expanse::region, text: str, opts) ([]T | error)
	fn unmarshal_from[T](m, rd: *reader) ([]T | error)
	fn columns_of[T](rd) (columns | done | error);  fn columns_in_order[T]() (columns | nomem)
	fn read_row[T](rd, m, c: *const columns) (T | done | error)
	fn marshal[T](rows: []const T, opts) (^str | nomem);  fn marshal_to[T](w, rows)
	fn write_header[T](w);  fn write_row[T](w, v: *const T)

Records are read as RFC 4180 has them: a field in double quotes may hold the separator, doubled quotes and line breaks (\r\n in a field is read as \n); blank lines are skipped, and lines starting with comment. A text and a file are read alike, a file a piece at a time. invalid says why (bare_quote, quote, field_count, duplicate_column), at which line and column, and on which line the record began. The writer quotes what needs it: the separator, quotes, line breaks, a leading space, and a record of one empty field, written "" so that it is not a blank line.

unmarshal reads rows as structs by the header's names, in any order; a column no field takes is left, and a field with no column is missing unless it is optional. Fields are str, bool (true/false, any case, or 1/0), integers, floats (with NaN, +Inf, -Inf), enums by member name, time::datetime, types with a text form (encoding::text_decoder, as uuid::uuid), and (T | void), empty for void. A field that is not its type's is a mismatch, with its line, column and field. Tags:

lora 
type person = struct {
	@csv(name = "age") years: int,
	@csv(format = "unix") joined: time::datetime,   // rfc3339, unix_ms, unix
	@csv(skip) cache: int,
}

xml — XML 1.0 with namespaces

Example: λexamples/xml.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
type options = struct {
	strict: bool = true,      // false: unknown entities kept, attributes with no quotes or value
	namespaces: bool = true,  // false: a name's space is its prefix, as written
	indent: str = "",         // writing: "" for one line
}
type name = struct { space: str, local: str }
type attr = struct { name: name, value: str }
type token = (start | end | chardata | comment | proc_inst | directive);
	// start { name, attrs }  end { name }  chardata { text }  comment { text }
	// proc_inst { target, text }  directive { text }
fn new_reader(text: str, opts) reader;  fn stream_reader(r: io::reader, opts) reader
	fn next(r: *reader) (token | done | invalid | io::failure)  // good until the next call
	fn skip(r) (void | ...)    // past the element just begun
	fn token_pos(r) (usize, usize);  fn depth(r) usize
fn new_writer(out: *^[]u8, opts) writer;  fn stream_writer(w: io::writer, opts) writer
	fn put_start(w, n: name, attrs: []const attr);  fn put_end(w)  // <a/> when empty
	fn put_text(w, s);  fn put_cdata(w, s);  fn put_comment(w, s)
	fn put_proc_inst(w, target, text);  fn put_directive(w, text);  fn put_header(w)
	fn flush(w);  fn finished(w) bool;  fn valid_name(s: str) bool
fn marshal[T](v: *const T, root: str = "", opts) (^str | invalid | nomem)
	fn marshal_to[T](w, v, root: str = "")
	fn unmarshal[T](m: *expanse::region, text: str, opts) (T | error)
	fn unmarshal_from[T](m, rd: *reader) (T | done | error)

Reading is strict, as XML is: one root element, names and the five entities and character references as the grammar has them, attribute values in quotes and never given twice, every element closed by its own end tag, <?xml ...?> only at the start, no -- in a comment, no prefix that is not bound. invalid says why and gives the line and column. Line breaks are read as \n, and in attribute values as spaces. With namespaces, a name's space is the URL its prefix (or the default) is bound to; xml is bound to XML_NAMESPACE. A text and a file are read alike.

The writer escapes text and attribute values, declares a default namespace where an element's space changes (a space of "" keeps the default), reuses a prefix bound in scope for an attribute's namespace or binds one, and refuses names, comments and characters XML does not have.

marshal and unmarshal write and read a struct as an element (named by root, or its type's name), field by field; elements no field takes are skipped, and a field nothing gave is left zero, void if optional, or missing if zero is not one of its type's values. Fields are strings, []u8, bool, integers, floats, enums by member name, time::datetime, types with a text form, structs, (T | void), and slices of these, an element each. Tags:

lora 
type person = struct {
	@xml(attr) id: int,                     // <person id="7">
	name: str,                              // <name>...</name>
	@xml("contact>phone") phones: []str,    // <contact><phone>1</phone><phone>2</phone></contact>
	@xml(chardata) text: str,               // the element's own text
	@xml(innerxml) body: str,               // its contents, as XML, as they are
	@xml(comment) note: str,                // <!--...-->
	@xml(omit_empty) nick: str,             // left out when "", 0, false, empty or void
	@xml(space = "urn:x") x: str,           // an element in a namespace
	@xml(skip) cache: int,
}

A type that writes or reads itself implements xml::marshaler or xml::unmarshaler. Tags that contradict one another, and two fields of one element or attribute name, are refused when compiling.

pack — values as bytes that describe themselves

Example: λexamples/pack.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
fn new_encoder(out: *^[]u8) encoder;  fn stream_encoder(w: io::writer) encoder
	fn encode[T](e: *encoder, v: *const T) (void | io::failure)
	fn flush(e: *encoder) (void | io::failure)
	fn marshal[T](v: *const T) (^[]u8 | nomem)       // a stream of one value
fn new_decoder(b: []const u8) decoder;  fn stream_decoder(r: io::reader) decoder
	fn decode[T](d: *decoder, m: *expanse::region) (T | done | error)
	fn unmarshal[T](m: *expanse::region, b: []const u8) (T | error)
type error = (invalid | missing | expanse::full | expanse::uncommitted | io::failure);

A stream describes each type once, before its first value: a struct's name and its fields' names and types, an enum's members' names, a slice's, array's or optional's elements. So a reader needs no schema but its own types, and the two ends may differ: struct fields are matched by name, a field the reader lacks is skipped, one the stream lacks is left zero (void if optional, missing if zero is not one of its type's values); enum members are matched by name; integers of any width and sign read as any other they fit, else out_of_range; an optional reads as what it holds. Values are bools, integers, floats, str, []u8, time::datetime, types with a text form, enums, structs, slices, arrays and optionals of them, and a type may hold itself through a slice. Strings and slices are put in the region. invalid says why and at which byte of the stream, and names the field. Each message is limited to MAX_MESSAGE bytes, and counts and lengths to what the message holds, so a stream can't make the reader take more memory than it sent. Values nested deeper than MAX_DEPTH (64) are invalid too, so a stream can't make it run out of stack either.

The bytes: a message is its length and a varint, a type's number before a value of it, or negated before its description. An int is a zigzag varint, a uint a uvarint, a float its bits reversed as a uvarint, a string or bytes its length and itself, a struct its non-zero fields as the difference from the last field's number and the value, then 0.

pem — keys and certificates as text

Example: λexamples/pem_asn1.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
type block = struct { kind: str, headers: ^[]header, bytes: ^[]u8 }
type header = struct { name: str, value: str }
fn decode(text: str) ((block, str) | void | invalid | nomem)   // the first block, and the rest
	fn decode_all(text: str) (^[]block | invalid | nomem)
	fn decode_kind(text: str, kind: str) (^[]block | invalid | nomem)
	fn finish(blocks: ^[]block) void           // wipes and frees
	fn encode(b: *const block) (^str | nomem);  fn append_encode(out: *^[]u8, b)

A block is the bytes between -----BEGIN kind----- and -----END kind-----, with headers (Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED) before a blank line if it has any. Text around blocks is skipped. The kind and headers are views of the text; the bytes are the block's own. What is decoded is never left in freed memory: buffers are made at their size and wiped, since PEM often holds keys. invalid says why (no_end, end_differs, bad_label, bad_header, bad_base64) and at which byte. Encoding writes base64 in lines of 64 characters.

asn1 — DER

Example: λexamples/pem_asn1.lora; a short one in encodings.md.

lora 
type value = struct { class: class, constructed: bool, tag: u32,
	body: []const u8, raw: []const u8, at: usize }
fn new_parser(der: []const u8) parser;  fn parse(der) (value | invalid)  // one element
	fn next(p: *parser) (value | done | invalid);  fn peek(p);  fn finished(p) bool
	fn enter(v: *const value) (parser | invalid)     // the elements inside
fn boolean(v) (bool | invalid);  fn integer(v) (i64 | invalid);  fn uinteger(v) (u64 | invalid)
	fn big(v) ([]const u8 | invalid);  fn big_unsigned(v);  fn enumerated(v);  fn read_null(v)
	fn octets(v) ([]const u8 | invalid);  fn bits(v) (bitstring | invalid)
	fn object_identifier(v) (oid | invalid);  fn string(v) (str | invalid)
	fn append_string(out: *^[]u8, v)   // BMPString and UniversalString too
	fn datetime(v) (time::datetime | invalid)  // UTCTime, GeneralizedTime
type oid = struct { arcs: [MAX_ARCS]u64, n: u8 }
	fn parse_oid(text: str) (oid | void);  fn oid_of(arcs: []const u64) (oid | void)
	fn oid_is(o, arcs: []const u64) bool;  fn oid_equal(a, b) bool;  fn append_oid_text(out, o)
fn new_writer(out: *^[]u8) writer
	fn begin(w, tag: u32);  fn begin_tagged(w, class, tag);  fn end(w)
	fn implicit(w, class, tag)   // the next element's tag
	fn put_bool, put_int, put_uint, put_big_unsigned, put_enum, put_null, put_octets,
	   put_bits, put_oid, put_string(w, string_kind, s), put_time(w, time_form, t),
	   put_element(w, class, constructed, tag, body), put_raw(w, der)
fn marshal[T](v: *const T) (^[]u8 | invalid | nomem);  fn marshal_to[T](w, v)
	fn unmarshal[T](r: *expanse::region, der: []const u8) (T | error)
	fn unmarshal_from[T](r: *expanse::region, p: *parser) (T | done | error)

Reading is strict, as DER is: a length or tag in more bytes than it needs, an indefinite length, an integer with a needless leading byte, a boolean other than 00 or ff, unused bits that are not zero, a time in any other form, a default written out: each is invalid, with the reason, the byte where the element begins, and the field being read. Ending a SET puts its elements in order, as DER has them.

marshal and unmarshal read and write a type whole, the code for it made while compiling: a struct is a SEQUENCE, a slice or array a SEQUENCE OF; bool, integers, enums (ENUMERATED), str (UTF8String unless the tag says), []u8 (OCTET STRING), bitstring, oid, time::datetime, raw (an element kept as it is), and (T | void) for what may be absent. A type with its own form implements asn1::marshaler and asn1::unmarshaler. Strings and slices are put in the region. Fields are tagged:

lora 
type extension = struct {
	id: asn1::oid,
	@asn1(default = false) critical: bool,
	value: []u8,
}
type tbs = struct {
	@asn1(tag = 0, explicit, default = 0) version: int,
	serial: asn1::raw,
	@asn1(sets) issuer: [][]attribute,          // SEQUENCE OF SET OF
	@asn1(tag = 3, explicit, optional) extensions: ([]extension | void),
	...
}

tag = n gives a context tag, IMPLICIT unless explicit, of the application or private class if asked; optional and default let a field be absent; set makes a SET or SET OF; string (printable, ia5, numeric, visible) and time (utc, generalized) choose the form; omit_empty leaves out an empty slice; skip leaves a field out. Tags that contradict one another are refused when compiling.

crypto — hashes, MACs, ciphers and signatures

All written in Lora, constant time where secrets are involved, with the processor's AES instructions (ARMv8 aese and aesd, x86 AES-NI) for AES.

lora 
type hash = interface { fn write([]u8) void; fn sum([]u8) []u8; fn reset() void;
	fn digest_size() usize; fn block_size() usize; }
fn sha256_new() sha256       // also sha224_new, sha384_new, sha512_new, sha512_224_new,
	                             // sha512_256_new, sha1_new, md5_new
	fn sha256_of(data: []u8) [32]u8   // and sha224_of, sha384_of, sha512_of, sha512_224_of,
	                                  // sha512_256_of, sha1_of, md5_of
	fn sha3_256_new() sha3;  fn sha3_256_of(data: []u8) [32]u8   // and 224, 384, 512
	fn shake128_new() shake;  fn shake256_new() shake;  fn shake128_of(data, out: []u8) void
	fn cshake128_new(n: []u8, s: []u8) shake;  fn cshake256_new(n, s) shake
	fn shake_write(h: *shake, data: []u8) void;  fn shake_read(h: *shake, out: []u8) void
	fn shake_reset(h: *shake) void
	fn blake2b_new(dlen: usize, key: []u8) (blake2b | bad_blake2)   // 1 to 64 bytes
	fn blake2b_new_with(dlen, key, salt: []u8, personal: []u8) (blake2b | bad_blake2)
	fn blake2s_new(dlen: usize, key: []u8) (blake2s | bad_blake2)   // 1 to 32 bytes; and _with
	fn blake2b_256_of, blake2b_512_of, blake2s_256_of(data: []u8) [N]u8
	fn hmac_new[H](h: H, key: []u8) hmac[H]       // hmac_write, hmac_sum; hmac_sha256/384/512
	fn hkdf_extract[H](h: H, salt: []u8, ikm: []u8, prk: []u8) []u8
	fn hkdf_expand[H](h: H, prk: []u8, info: []u8, out: []u8) (void | too_long)
	fn pbkdf2[H](h: H, password: []u8, salt: []u8, rounds: u32, out: []u8) void
	fn argon2id(password, salt: []u8, time: u32, memory: u32, lanes: u32, out: []u8) (void | bad_argon2 | nomem)
	fn argon2(v: argon2_variant, password, salt, secret, ad: []u8, time, memory, lanes: u32, out) ...
	fn scrypt(password, salt: []u8, n: u64, r: u32, p: u32, out: []u8) (void | bad_scrypt | nomem)
	fn bcrypt_hash(password: []u8, cost: u32) ([60]u8 | bad_bcrypt)          // $2b$, a random salt
	fn bcrypt_check(hash, password: []u8) (void | mismatch | invalid_bcrypt)
	fn bcrypt_cost(hash: []u8) (u32 | invalid_bcrypt)
	fn chacha20poly1305_seal(key: *[32]u8, nonce: *[12]u8, aad: []u8, data: []u8) [16]u8
	fn chacha20poly1305_open(key: *[32]u8, nonce: *[12]u8, aad: []u8, data: []u8, tag: []u8) (void | forged)
	fn xchacha20poly1305_seal(key: *[32]u8, nonce: *[24]u8, aad, data) [16]u8   // and _open
	fn secretbox_seal(key: *[32]u8, nonce: *[24]u8, data: []u8) [16]u8         // NaCl; and _open
	fn box_seal(their_public, my_private: *[32]u8, nonce: *[24]u8, data) [16]u8  // and box_open
	fn box_shared(their_public, my_private: *[32]u8) [32]u8
	fn box_seal_anonymous(recipient: *[32]u8, data: []u8) ([32]u8, [16]u8)   // and _open_anonymous
	fn aes_new(key: []u8) (aes | bad_key)        // 16, 24 or 32 bytes
	fn aes_encrypt(a: *aes, in: *[16]u8, out: *[16]u8) void;  fn aes_decrypt(...)
	fn aes_gcm_seal(a: *aes, nonce: *[12]u8, aad: []u8, data: []u8) [16]u8
	fn aes_gcm_open(a: *aes, nonce: *[12]u8, aad: []u8, data: []u8, tag: []u8) (void | forged)
	fn aes_gcm_seal_with(a, nonce: []u8, aad, data, tag: []u8) void   // any nonce, 12-16 byte tag
	fn aes_gcm_open_with(a, nonce: []u8, aad, data, tag: []u8) (void | forged)
	fn aes_gcm_seal_random(a, nonce: *[12]u8, aad, data) [16]u8      // nonce made and given
	fn des_new(key: []u8) (des | bad_des_key);  fn des3_new(key: []u8) (des3 | bad_des_key)
	fn rc4_new(key: []u8) (rc4 | bad_rc4_key);  fn rc4_xor(c: *rc4, data: []u8) void   // broken
	fn rc4_wipe(c: *rc4) void
